A food’s sweet taste, not just its calorie count, determines both how the metabolism reacts and the brain’s understanding of its nutritional content, new research suggests.
“Calories are only half of the equation; sweet taste perception is the other half.”
The findings may explain the association between artificial sweeteners and diabetes.
In nature, sweetness signals the presence of energy and its intensity reflects the amount of energy present. When a beverage is either too sweet or not sweet enough for the amount of calories it contains, the metabolic response and the signal that communicates nutritional value to the brain are disrupted, according to the study published in the journal Current Biology.
“A calorie is not a calorie,” says senior author Dana Small, professor of psychiatry at the Yale University School of Medicine.
The new study shows that sweetness helps to determine how calories are metabolized and signaled to the brain. When sweetness and calories are matched, the calories are metabolized, and this is registered by brain reward circuits.
When a “mismatch” occurs, however, the calories fail to trigger the body’s metabolism and the reward circuits in the brain fail to register that calories have been consumed.
“In other words, the assumption that more calories trigger greater metabolic and brain response is wrong,” Small says. “Calories are only half of the equation; sweet taste perception is the other half.”
Small noted that many processed foods contain such mismatches—such as a yogurt with low calorie sweeteners.
“Our bodies evolved to efficiently use the energy sources available in nature,” Small says. “Our modern food environment is characterized by energy sources our bodies have never seen before.”
The National Institutes of Health and PepsiCo provided the primary funding for the study.
Source: Yale University
rewrite:
Emerging research indicates that a food's sweet taste, independent of its caloric content, plays a critical role in determining both metabolic responses and the brain's perception of nutritional value. This suggests that caloric content alone is an insufficient predictor of physiological processing. As senior author Dana Small, a professor of psychiatry at the Yale University School of Medicine, states, "Calories are only half of the equation; sweet taste perception is the other half." These findings may provide a mechanistic explanation for observed epidemiological links between the consumption of artificial sweeteners and metabolic disorders such as diabetes.

In natural environments, sweetness typically functions as a reliable signal for the presence of metabolic energy, with its intensity correlating with the amount of available calories. The study, published in *Current Biology*, demonstrates that when this relationship is disrupted—that is, when a beverage's sweetness is not congruent with its actual caloric load—both the metabolic response and the neural signaling of nutritional value are impaired. Specifically, when sweetness and calories are matched, calories are effectively metabolized and this process is accurately registered by the brain's reward circuits. Conversely, a "mismatch" results in a failure to trigger normal metabolism and a failure of these same reward circuits to recognize caloric consumption.

This challenges the conventional assumption that a higher caloric load invariably elicits a proportionally greater metabolic and neural response. Small notes that such mismatches are prevalent in modern processed foods, citing the example of a yogurt sweetened with low-calorie alternatives. She contextualizes this within an evolutionary framework: "Our bodies evolved to efficiently use the energy sources available in nature. Our modern food environment is characterized by energy sources our bodies have never seen before." The primary funding for this research was provided by the National Institutes of Health and PepsiCo.

APRIL 24, 2018 — Rolls-Royce has signed a contract to deliver ship design and an extensive range of equipment to a 70 m long stern trawler to be built for Olympic Seafood based in Fosnavåg, Norway.
The vessel is to be built by Turkey's Cemre Shipyard. The shipbuilding contract includes an option for a second vessel of the same type for Olympic Seafood.
Shipowner Stig Remøy, said: "This is a new and modern generation of trawler. The planning and design has been conducted under the headline smarter, greener and safer. Low energy consumption and reduced emissions make the concept a perfect fit for our strategy of sustainable ocean harvesting. Rolls-Royce has played a central role in the development of our new ship."
The vessel will be of type NVC 370 with a low resistant hull design that meets increased demands for fuel efficiency combined with good sea keeping.
Monrad Hide, Rolls-Royce, Vice President Sales, said: "It's a pleasure working with ambitious shipping owners such as Stig Remøy and his team. We've designed a highly efficient trawler that will be equipped with a package of power and propulsion, electrical and automation systems that will deliver benefits to both the owner and the environment, as well as safety and good working conditions for the crew."
The equipment to be delivered by Rolls-Royce includes a Bergen B33:45 diesel engine as part of a hybrid propulsion system that can deliver both mechanical and diesel-electric drive to the vessel's Promas integrated rudder and propeller system. A Hybrid Shaft Generator (HSG) ensures optimum propeller and engine efficiency by running both at their most efficient point.
Rolls-Royce deliveries will also include its latest deck winches, driven by a permanent magnet electric motor.
The new vessel is designed for bottom trawling as well as pelagic trawling. It will have a modern factory deck arrangement to handle and freeze both white fish and shrimp and ensure a high quality catch.
The vessel is expected to be delivered from the shipyard in 2020.

The vessel is to be constructed for Olympic Seafood, based in Fosnavåg, Norway, at the Cemre Shipyard in Turkey. The shipbuilding agreement includes an option for a second vessel of identical specification for the same owner.

Stig Remøy, the shipowner, stated that the vessel represents a new and modern generation of trawler. He emphasized that its planning and design were guided by the principles of being smarter, greener, and safer. The concept’s low energy consumption and reduced emissions align with the company’s strategy for sustainable ocean harvesting, a development in which Rolls-Royce is reported to have played a central role.

The vessel will be of the NVC 370 type, featuring a low-resistance hull design engineered to meet heightened demands for fuel efficiency while maintaining good seakeeping performance. Monrad Hide, Vice President of Sales at Rolls-Royce, commented on the collaboration with ambitious owners like Remøy, noting the design of a highly efficient trawler. It will be equipped with an integrated package of power and propulsion, electrical, and automation systems intended to deliver operational benefits, environmental advantages, and enhanced safety and working conditions for the crew.

Rolls-Royce’s equipment delivery will include a Bergen B33:45 diesel engine within a hybrid propulsion system. This system is capable of delivering both mechanical and diesel-electric drive to the vessel’s Promas integrated rudder and propeller system. A Hybrid Shaft Generator (HSG) will be incorporated to optimize propeller and engine efficiency by maintaining both at their most efficient operational points. Further deliveries will encompass the latest deck winches, driven by permanent magnet electric motors.

Designed for both bottom and pelagic trawling, the vessel will feature a modern factory deck arrangement to process and freeze white fish and shrimp, thereby ensuring high-quality catch. Delivery from the shipyard is anticipated in 2020.

Louisiana lawmakers could soon debate whether a teacher killed in a school shooting should get the same benefits as an officer or firefighter killed in the line of duty.
The bill by Sen. Neil Riser, R-Columbia, puts teachers on par with first responders, giving their families access to survivor benefits. For example, the state would pay out $250,000 to the spouse or children of the school worker killed.
Riser says the death could be the result of anything from a school shooting to stepping in to break up a schoolyard fight.
"Who would ever thought we'd be listing our teachers as first responders, but as it currently stands right now, if anything goes wrong, they are the first responders to the situations we have," Riser said.
Everyone from elementary school staff to a college professor is included under the bill. The legislation is backed by the Louisiana Federation of Teachers. The bill was scheduled for a committee hearing Monday, but did not come up for consideration.
RELATED: La. lawmakers draft bills letting teachers conceal carry in the classroom
The deadly Valentine's Day shooting at a Florida high school inspired several pieces of legislation at the state capitol during the 2018 session. Several bills allow teachers to be armed in the classroom, while others put new restrictions on gun sales.
Copyright 2018 WAFB. All rights reserved.
rewrite:
Louisiana legislators may soon consider a bill that would grant teachers killed in school shootings equivalent benefits to those provided to police officers or firefighters who die in the line of duty. Proposed by Senator Neil Riser (R-Columbia), the legislation classifies educators as first responders, thereby making their families eligible for survivor benefits, including a $250,000 payment from the state to the spouse or children of a deceased school employee. Senator Riser explained that such fatalities could result from incidents ranging from a school shooting to intervention in a physical altercation on school grounds. He noted, “Who would have ever thought we would be listing our teachers as first responders, but as it currently stands, if anything goes wrong, they are the first to respond to these situations.”

The bill encompasses all educational staff, from elementary school personnel to university professors, and has received endorsement from the Louisiana Federation of Teachers. Although scheduled for a committee hearing on Monday, the measure was not brought forward for discussion. This proposal emerges alongside other legislative efforts inspired by the 2018 shooting at a Florida high school, which have included bills both permitting teachers to carry concealed firearms in classrooms and imposing new restrictions on firearm sales.

LANSING, Mich. (AP) — A high-ranking Michigan State University official involved in the board of trustees' plan said Tuesday that former Gov. John Engler will be named interim president.
The official told The Associated Press that the board will vote to hire Engler on Wednesday amid the fallout over sexual assaults committed by former school sports doctor Larry Nassar. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity because the decision had not been publicly announced.
President Lou Anna Simon resigned last week, and the board named Bill Beekman as acting president.
Engler, a Michigan State graduate, served as Michigan's Republican governor from 1990 through 2002. He will lead the school as it confronts civil lawsuits filed by more than 100 women and girls, and investigations by the state attorney general, the NCAA and Congress.
Nassar was sentenced to 40 to 175 years in prison last week at the end of an extraordinary seven-day hearing at which more than 150 women and girls said he had molested them under the guise of medical treatment. Nassar worked for Michigan State and USA Gymnastics, treating numerous athletes including some Olympians. Victims blamed Michigan State, USA Gymnastics and the U.S. Olympic Committee for not doing more earlier to stop him.
Reacting to several media reports that Engler will be named to the post, State House Speaker Tom Leonard, a DeWitt Republican, said in a statement that the former governor is the "right choice."
"He is a strong leader with a proven track record of reform, and the school needs someone who is able to come in from the outside, stand up to the status quo and make immediate changes," he said in a statement. "I look forward to working with the interim president on new reforms that will better protect women, the students at MSU and the local community."
rewrite:
In a development reported on Tuesday, a senior Michigan State University administrator involved with the board of trustees’ planning indicated that former Governor John Engler will be appointed as the institution’s interim president. According to this official, who spoke to The Associated Press under condition of anonymity due to the pending nature of the announcement, the board is scheduled to formally vote on Engler’s appointment on Wednesday. This action occurs amidst ongoing repercussions from the sexual assault crimes committed by former university and USA Gymnastics physician Larry Nassar.

The university’s leadership transition follows last week’s resignation of President Lou Anna Simon and the subsequent designation of Bill Beekman as acting president. Engler, an alumnus of Michigan State University who served as Michigan’s Republican governor from 1990 to 2002, will assume leadership while the institution addresses multiple civil lawsuits filed by over one hundred women and girls, alongside investigations conducted by the state attorney general, the NCAA, and Congress.

Nassar was sentenced last week to 40 to 175 years in prison following a seven-day hearing during which more than 150 victims provided testimony detailing assaults perpetrated under the guise of medical treatment. Victims have cited systemic failures, criticizing Michigan State University, USA Gymnastics, and the U.S. Olympic Committee for not intervening earlier to halt Nassar’s misconduct.

Responding to media reports of the impending appointment, Michigan House Speaker Tom Leonard (R-DeWitt) issued a statement endorsing Engler as the “right choice.” Leonard characterized Engler as a strong leader with a demonstrated history of reform, stating the university requires an external figure capable of challenging the status quo and implementing prompt changes. He further expressed anticipation for collaborating with the interim president on reforms aimed at enhancing protections for women, Michigan State University students, and the broader community.

SYDNEY, March 28 Australian sandalwood plantation group Quintis Ltd said on Tuesday its managing director has resigned and will consider making a takeover offer for the company together with an unnamed international group.
The move follows the publication last week of a highly negative report by short-seller Glaucus Research Group that knocked shares in Quintis down 24 percent, taking its market capitalistion to A$430 million ($328 million).
Quintis, formerly known as TFS Corp., is one of the last remaining publicly-listed managed investment schemes in Australia and has Indian and Australian sandalwood plantations. Oil from the trees is sold to India and China for fragrances, cosmetics and medicinal uses.
Shares in the company jumped 10 percent in early trade on Tuesday on news of a potential bid. Managing director Frank Wilson owns about 13 percent of the company and topped up his shareholding with a A$59,000 investment last week when the company came under attack from Glaucus.
The collapses of Timbercorp Ltd and several other large forestry investment schemes, starting in 2009, drew widespread criticism of an investment model which frequently involved small investors borrowing money for high-risk operations.
In response to a query from the Australian Securities Exchange, Quintis said on Monday its biggest customer in China, Shanghai Richer Link, had not ordered any shipments this year.
Chairman Dalton Gooding said in a statement on Tuesday that the fundamentals of the business remained strong, but the company was dealing with "a number of issues" that had affected its share price.
Any offer for Quintis would be independently assessed on whether it was in the best interests of all shareholders, he said.
Wilson said he had received several approaches over the years from parties interested in bidding for Quintis, although none had progressed to a formal proposal.
"More recently, I have been contacted by a well-funded party with what I believe to be a serious approach," he said in a statement. "It is my intention to fully assess this confidential approach and any others, unencumbered by my duties and responsibilities as managing director." ($1 = 1.3123 Australian dollars) (Reporting by Jamie Freed; Editing by Richard Pullin)
rewrite:
On March 28, in Sydney, Quintis Ltd, an Australian sandalwood plantation enterprise, announced the resignation of its Managing Director, Frank Wilson. The company further disclosed that Mr. Wilson, in conjunction with an undisclosed international consortium, is contemplating the formulation of a takeover bid for Quintis. This development follows the recent publication of a critical report by short-selling firm Glaucus Research Group, which precipitated a 24 percent decline in Quintis’s share price last week, reducing its market capitalization to approximately A$430 million (US$328 million).

Quintis, previously named TFS Corp., operates Indian and Australian sandalwood plantations, with its derived oil supplied to fragrance, cosmetic, and pharmaceutical industries in India and China. The company represents one of the few remaining publicly-listed managed investment schemes in Australia. News of a potential acquisition prompted a 10 percent surge in the company’s shares during early trading on Tuesday. Mr. Wilson, who holds an approximate 13 percent equity stake, augmented his position with a A$59,000 investment last week amidst the market downturn following Glaucus’s report.

The announcement occurs within a historical context of scrutiny toward forestry investment schemes in Australia, notably following the collapse of Timbercorp Ltd and other entities beginning in 2009. These failures prompted criticism of investment models that often involved retail investors utilizing leverage for high-risk agricultural projects. In a separate disclosure on Monday, Quintis responded to an Australian Securities Exchange inquiry by confirming that its primary Chinese client, Shanghai Richer Link, has not placed any orders for the current year.

Quintis Chairman Dalton Gooding issued a statement on Tuesday asserting that the company’s fundamental business operations remain robust, while acknowledging it is addressing “a number of issues” that have adversely affected its share price. He emphasized that any formal offer for the company would be subjected to independent evaluation to determine its alignment with the best interests of all shareholders. Mr. Wilson noted he has received several informal expressions of interest in Quintis over previous years, none of which materialized into a formal proposal. It is my intention to fully assess this confidential approach and any others, unencumbered by my duties and responsibilities as managing director.”

We all know Uranus has long been the butt of many jokes, and it doesn’t seem like the planet is going to be getting any slack now: a team of British researchers has revealed that it reeks of fart fumes.
The findings, published recently in the Nature Astronomy journal, reveal that Uranus' upper atmosphere smells like rotten eggs, the signature scent of the colorless, flammable hydrogen sulfide gas it is made up of.
© Sputnik / Alina Polyanina Planetesimal: Scientists Find Traces of a Long-Dead Planet
"If an unfortunate human were ever to descend through Uranus' cloud, they would be met with very unpleasant and odiferous conditions," one of the report's authors, Patrick Irwin, told BBC recently.
But of course, the smell's not the worst of the Uranus experience. "Suffocation and exposure in the negative 200 degrees Celsius [minus 328 degrees Fahrenheit] atmosphere made of mostly hydrogen, helium and methane would take its toll long before the smell," Irwin added. Chances are, no one could live long enough to actually get a whiff of Uranus' stinkiness.
The researchers detected the foul smells — er, chemical composition — using the Near-Infrared Integral Field Spectrometer (NIFS) of Hawaii's Gemini North telescope, which sits on the Mauna Kea volcano in Hawaii.
The scientists used the 26.5-foot telescope to examine samples of reflected sunlight from Uranus' high atmosphere, which showed that hydrogen sulfide had absorbed some wavelengths from the sun.
According to Leigh Fletcher, a senior research fellow in planetary science at the University of Leicester in England and co-author of the study, the hydrogen sulfide composition in the upper atmosphere of Uranus is different than that of Jupiter and Saturn, where ammonia is present in large amounts instead.
rewrite:
Recent findings published in *Nature Astronomy* have provided new insights into the atmospheric composition of Uranus, confirming the presence of hydrogen sulfide in its upper cloud layers. This colorless, flammable gas, known for its characteristic odor reminiscent of rotten eggs, was detected through spectroscopic analysis of sunlight reflected from the planet’s atmosphere. Utilizing the Near-Infrared Integral Field Spectrometer (NIFS) on the 8.1-meter Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, researchers examined absorption lines in the near-infrared spectrum, identifying specific wavelengths absorbed by hydrogen sulfide molecules.

As Patrick Irwin, a co-author of the study, noted, direct human exposure to these atmospheric conditions would be profoundly inhospitable. Beyond the pronounced olfactory discomfort, any hypothetical descent through Uranus’s clouds would involve lethal hazards, including suffocation in an atmosphere composed primarily of hydrogen, helium, and methane, coupled with extreme temperatures approaching –200 degrees Celsius (–328 degrees Fahrenheit). Consequently, survival would be impossible long before the odor could be perceived.

The detection of hydrogen sulfide distinguishes Uranus from the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn, whose upper atmospheres contain abundant ammonia rather than significant concentrations of hydrogen sulfide. According to Leigh Fletcher, a senior research fellow at the University of Leicester and study co-author, this compositional difference offers important clues regarding the formation and evolution of ice giants within the solar system. These observations not only refine our understanding of planetary atmospheres but also contribute to broader models of solar system formation and atmospheric chemistry.

Two bodies were found in Indiana during a search for two missing girls on Tuesday, PEOPLE confirms.
A spokesman for the Carroll County Sheriff’s Department would not confirm if the bodies discovered were identified those of missing 13-year-olds Liberty German and Abigail Williams.
The bodies were found Tuesday at about 12:15 p.m. and the case is an ongoing investigation, the spokesman tells PEOPLE.
“We are investigating this as a crime scene,” Indiana State Police Sgt. Kim Riley said at a press conference shortly after 2 p.m. Tuesday, according to the IndyStar. “We suspect foul play.”
Fox 59, a local news station, reports that police have not called off the search for German and Williams.
The girls were determined to be missing on Monday, hours after they had been dropped off to go hiking earlier that day, according to the Associated Press.
The AP reports that the bodies were found Tuesday on the edge of a creek near an abandoned railroad bridge where German and Williams were dropped off.

Indiana State Police Sergeant Kim Riley stated at a press conference shortly after 2:00 p.m., as reported by the IndyStar, "We are investigating this as a crime scene," adding, "We suspect foul play." Per local station Fox 59, law enforcement has not terminated the search for German and Williams. The Associated Press notes the girls were reported missing on Monday, several hours after being deposited for a hiking excursion earlier that day. The AP further specifies the bodies were found Tuesday near the bank of a creek adjacent to an abandoned railroad bridge, the location where the pair had initially been dropped off.

NEW YORK — John Mellencamp sank to his knees in support of the Black Lives Matter movement after a performance on “Late Show With Stephen Colbert" on Thursday evening.
The musician performed his song "Easy Target" to which was originally released on the eve of President Trump's inauguration in January 2017.
The song addresses racial inequality and Mellencamp references the Black Lives Matter movement with his lyrics such as:
"So Black Lives Matter, who we tryin' to kid. Here's an easy target. Don't matter, never did."
"All of us are created equal - equally beneath me and you."
At the end of his performance, Mellencamp knelt and lifted his right fist into the air.
The song comes from Mellencamp’s album “Sad Clowns & Hillbillies,” which came out late last year.
You can watch his performance below.
The movement was started by former 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick last season. He took a knee during the National Anthem to silently protest racial inequality and treatment of black Americans, particularly by police.
The protests prompted President Donald Trump to tweet that NFL owner should "fire or suspend" players that "disrespect" the "flag & country."
“Taking the knee started purely and simply as a protest of racial and social injustice,” Mellencamp told The Associated Press. “Sadly it was politicized by the current administration. The song is simple and the protest is pure.”

During a Thursday evening appearance on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert," musician John Mellencamp concluded a performance by kneeling and raising a clenched fist, a gesture aligning himself with the Black Lives Matter movement. His performance featured the song "Easy Target," a track initially released in January 2017 coinciding with the presidential inauguration. The lyrics explicitly engage with themes of racial inequality, stating: "So Black Lives Matter, who we tryin' to kid. Here's an easy target. Don't matter, never did," and "All of us are created equal - equally beneath me and you." The song is included on his 2017 album "Sad Clowns & Hillbillies."

This act of kneeling directly references protests initiated by former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick, who knelt during the national anthem to highlight racial injustice and police brutality against African Americans. These demonstrations elicited a critical response from President Donald Trump, who suggested NFL owners should penalize players for such actions. In a statement to The Associated Press, Mellencamp clarified the intent behind the symbol, noting, “Taking the knee started purely and simply as a protest of racial and social injustice. Sadly it was politicized by the current administration. The song is simple and the protest is pure.” His performance thus served as a deliberate artistic and political statement reaffirming the movement's core principles.

DETROIT (AP) - Consumer Reports is now recommending Tesla's Model 3 compact electric car after a company software update improved its poor braking performance.
The magazine says the wireless update of antilock braking software cut 19 feet from the car's stopping distance from 60 miles per hour.
A previous test found that it took 152 feet for the car to stop from 60. That was the longest braking distance of any modern car the magazine has tested.
But in a test after the update, the stopping distance fell to 133 feet. Consumer Reports says that's typical for a compact luxury car.
The improved braking raised the car's score high enough for it to be a recommended buy. But the magazine still has concerns over wind noise and the touch-screen controls.

rewrite: In a recent evaluation, Consumer Reports has reinstated its recommendation for the Tesla Model 3 compact electric vehicle. This follows a corrective software update issued by Tesla, which substantially enhanced the vehicle's previously substandard braking performance. Initial testing had recorded a stopping distance of 152 feet, the longest observed in any contemporary vehicle assessed by the magazine. Image copyright Reuters
Big Ben's famous chimes will fall silent until 2021 next week to allow essential repair works to take place.
The bongs will sound for the final time at midday on Monday before being disconnected to allow the clock and surrounding tower to be restored.
The Great Bell has sounded on the hour for 157 years.
It last fell silent in 2007 and before that, for major refurbishments between 1983 and 1985.
Parliamentary authorities said stopping Big Ben - the commonly used name for the Palace of Westminster's Elizabeth Tower - would protect workers carrying out the repairs.
It will still sound for important events including New Year's Eve and Remembrance Sunday.
The clock's keeper, Steve Jaggs, said Big Ben falling silent was a "significant milestone" in the project to restore the tower.
"This essential programme of works will safeguard the clock on a long term basis, as well as protecting and preserving its home - the Elizabeth Tower," he added.
Big Ben basics
Image copyright PA
Formally known as the Great Bell, it forms part of the Great Clock in the Elizabeth Tower - commonly known as Big Ben
It weighs 13.7 tonnes and stands 96 ft tall
Every hour it strikes an E note, and every 15 minutes four "quarter bells" chime
To stop the chimes, the striking hammers will be locked until 2021
The landmark Elizabeth Tower is said to be the most photographed building in the UK.
Scaffolding is up and work has already started to repair and redecorate the interior, improve health and safety and fire protection systems, and make it more energy efficient.
During the repair work, an electric motor will drive the clock hands until the main mechanism has been restored, so it will continue to tell the time.
However, the faces will need to be temporarily covered while the clock itself is undergoing maintenance.
The wider Parliamentary estate is also in need of repair, and a multi-billion pound programme involving MPs temporarily relocating has been put forward.
rewrite:
The renowned chimes of Big Ben, the Great Bell housed within the Palace of Westminster’s Elizabeth Tower, will cease for an extended period commencing next week to facilitate essential conservation works. The final auditory signal will occur at midday on Monday, after which the striking mechanism will be disconnected to enable comprehensive restoration of both the clock and its architectural setting. This suspension follows a historical pattern, as the bell previously fell silent in 2007 and, prior to that, during a major refurbishment undertaken between 1983 and 1985. Parliamentary authorities have indicated that halting the chimes—a measure applying to the clock’s hourly and quarterly signals—is necessary to ensure the safety of personnel conducting the repairs, which are projected to continue until 2021. Notwithstanding this extended silence, the bell will be temporarily reactivated to mark significant national occasions, such as New Year’s Eve and Remembrance Sunday.

Steve Jaggs, the Clock Mechanic in charge of the Great Clock, has described the impending silence as a “significant milestone” within the broader restoration project. He emphasised that this essential programme is designed to safeguard the clock’s long-term operation while concurrently preserving the structural and historical integrity of the Elizabeth Tower itself. The landmark tower, frequently cited as the United Kingdom’s most photographed building, has already been partially enveloped in scaffolding. Ongoing work includes interior repair and redecoration, enhancements to health and safety and fire protection systems, and improvements to energy efficiency. During this period, an electric motor will maintain the movement of the clock hands to ensure continued timekeeping, although the clock faces will be temporarily obscured during direct maintenance of the mechanism.

This specific restoration forms part of a more extensive, multi-billion pound renovation programme required across the Parliamentary estate. Proposals associated with this wider initiative include the temporary relocation of Members of Parliament to allow for necessary structural and systemic upgrades.

BRUSSELS, Feb 2 (Reuters) - The next negotiation round between Britain and the European Union on the terms of divorce and the transition period that is to follow will run from Tuesday to Friday next week, the EU’s chief negotiator Michel Barnier said.
The round will tackle issues linked to the governance of the withdrawal agreement, the border between Northern Ireland and Ireland and the transition period, Barnier said on Twitter, noting that he will first spend Monday in London, where he will meet his opposite number, Brexit Secretary David Davis.
On Friday, there will be a meeting in Brussels at the level of coordinators’ of the negotiations which will sum up the round and at which Britain will update the EU on its request for a close future trade relationship.
EU and British officials, asked if this meant that Britain would spell out its demands in detail, declined to comment. (Reporting By Jan Strupczewski in Brussels and Andrew MacAskill in London; Editing by Alastair Macdonald)
rewrite: The next round of negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union concerning the terms of withdrawal and the subsequent transition period is scheduled to commence on Tuesday of the forthcoming week and conclude on Friday, according to a statement by the EU’s chief negotiator, Michel Barnier. As indicated in a social media announcement, the agenda for this session will address matters pertaining to the governance of the withdrawal agreement, the border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, and the transition framework. Prior to the negotiations, Barnier will meet in London on Monday with his counterpart, Brexit Secretary David Davis. A concluding meeting at the level of negotiation coordinators will be held in Brussels on Friday to summarize the round; during this meeting, the United Kingdom is expected to provide further details regarding its proposal for a future close trading relationship with the EU. When queried on whether this signifies a detailed articulation of British demands, officials from both parties declined to comment.

FORT COLLINS, Colo. — Caleb Martin had 26 points, Lindsey Drew added 16 and eight rebounds and Nevada turned back Colorado State 76-67 on Saturday night to put the finishing touches on a rough day for the Rams.
Colorado State lost its sixth straight on a day that head coach Larry Eustachy was put on administrative leave over questions about his conduct.
Kendall Stephens added 15 points for the Wolf Pack (20-4, 9-1 Mountain West Conference), who struggled to find their shooting touch from the field, but connected on 26 of 32 free throws.
Che Bob and Anthony Bonner paced the Rams (10-15, 3-9) with 13 points each, while Deion James added 12 points and eight rebounds.
The Rams trailed just 37-35 at halftime and used two James’ 3-pointers to grab a 41-40 lead early in the second half. But Stephens twice connected from beyond the arc and Martin added a layup to cap an 11-1 run for a 51-43 lead. Martin scored eight in the final 3:13 to seal it.

Despite trailing only 37-35 at halftime and briefly taking a 41-40 lead early in the second half, Colorado State succumbed to an 11-1 Nevada run. Martin sealed the victory by scoring eight points in the final 3:13.

The Heat donated $20,000 to D.A. Dorsey Technical College after the school was broken into and burglarized earlier this month. The extra help is all part of The Heat’s Random Acts of Heat initiative.

Of course, Trump can’t denounce this type of bullsh*t because these are the same people who voted him into the White House. Analysts suggest President Trump's muted condemnation stems from a perceived political alignment with segments of his electorate. This pattern is consistent with his historical reluctance to explicitly repudiate figures such as former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke. Yet another parenting debate has been sparked on Mumsnet by a mother asking a question.
The mum queried whether she should let her daughter stay in bed and be late for school because she was tired.
Taking to the popular forum, which has been the source of many fierce debates over its lifetime, the mum wrote: "Am I being unreasonable to leave the child in bed and be late for school?
"She's hardly slept this past week and she's like a little zombie by about 4pm."
The mum's username is "Singlebutmarried".
And her post sparked a slew of responses, reports the Liverpool Echo.
Users were instantly divided.
SuperMoonIsKeepingMeUpToo said: "If reception I might have considered it, but at seven I would say she needs to know that she goes to school unless ill. She can come home and collapse at 4pm!"
And user 'speakout' said that she let her kids have a 'monthly duvet day' when they could choose a day to have off school.
But others were quick to disagree, Lizzie48 posted: "I can understand why you might consider it, but it isn't something I would do, simply because DD1 (Darling daughter one) in particular would see it as a precedent and keep asking for another day off.
"We've always made it clear to both our DDs (Darling Daughters) that they only miss school if they're unwell."

Similarly, MrsSnootyPants2018 said: "I think you need to teach your child the importance of going to bed and sleeping.
"It may also be that she needs an earlier bedtime. At seven-years-old it's still your responsibility as her parent to make sure she sleeps enough."
Singlebutmarried later commented on the forum saying that she let her daughter wake up by herself and they made it to school five minutes late.
She said: "Far less grumpy than when woken."
rewrite:
A recent discussion on the popular online forum Mumsnet has reignited debates concerning parental discretion in matters of school attendance. The conversation was initiated by a user identified as “Singlebutmarried,” who presented a dilemma regarding her seven-year-old daughter. The mother detailed that her child had slept very little over the preceding week, becoming noticeably fatigued by the afternoon, and inquired whether it would be unreasonable to allow her daughter to remain in bed, even if it resulted in a late arrival at school.

The query prompted a substantial and divided response from the forum’s community. One perspective, articulated by a user named SuperMoonIsKeepingMeUpToo, emphasized the importance of routine, suggesting that at seven years old, a child should understand attendance is mandatory barring illness, with rest deferred until after school. A similar viewpoint was offered by Lizzie48, who expressed concern that such an allowance could establish an undesirable precedent, leading to repeated requests for non-attendance. This user clarified that within their own family, the policy is to miss school only in cases of genuine illness.

Conversely, an alternative approach was suggested by user ‘speakout,’ who described implementing a scheduled “monthly duvet day,” allowing children a pre-arranged day of absence. Others focused on underlying sleep hygiene. For instance, MrsSnootyPants2018 proposed that the core issue might be an insufficiently early bedtime, noting that ensuring adequate sleep for a seven-year-old remains a fundamental parental responsibility.

Following the discussion, the original poster provided an update. She reported allowing her daughter to wake naturally, resulting in a school arrival only five minutes behind schedule. The mother observed that this approach yielded a far less irritable child compared to mornings when she was forcibly awakened. This outcome highlights the practical compromise sometimes negotiated between institutional expectations and individual familial circumstances, a recurrent theme in contemporary parenting discourse.

MARK CARRINGTON insists Wrexham will click and start creating chances.
Wrexham suffered a second defeat in three outings as the Reds lost 1-0 against Dover.
Despite making a promising start, the Reds rarely threatened a goal after going behind in the 18th minute, carving out few opportunities, but Carrington is adamant things will change.
“We haven’t created a lot of chances but it will come,” said Carrington, the Reds’ vice captain and longest serving player in Dean Keates’ squad.
“You always go through spells in the season and then you end up hitting someone for five along the way and it will all be forgotten.
“I wouldn’t worry about it too much, it is still early days.”
Keates has revamped the squad over the summer but Carrington, pictured right, refuses to use the changes as an excuse.
“It is difficult but we have got to adjust fast,” said Carrington. “We can’t use that as an excuse, we have got to think fast and get it sorted.”
Wrexham were aiming to build on their first win of the season against Maidenhead United but despite making a lively start, had no answer to Ryan Bird’s opener.
“We started not bad the first 15 minutes and put them on the back foot,” said Carrington.
“After they scored, we tried to get back into it but it didn’t really look like it was going to be our day.
“Dover are good at what they do. They get it forward quickly and put you under pressure. We will just have to go again tomorrow against Gateshead.”
On the goal, with the ball falling kindly for Bird in the area, Carrington said: “It was another lucky ricochet like Tuesday and it fell to him in the box which you can’t really do a lot about.
“We have just got to stick our chances away, the couple that we had first half early doors.
“The first game was 0-0 written all over it, just one chance. Today again was just one chance they had and scored.
“Tuesday was a great win for us, it is just fine margins at the moment but I am sure we will iron them out; when they start falling our way then we will go on a bit of a run.”
rewrite:
Mark Carrington maintains that Wrexham will soon find their rhythm and begin to generate offensive opportunities. This assertion follows a second defeat in three matches, a 1-0 loss to Dover Athletic. Despite an initially promising opening period, the team offered minimal threat after conceding in the 18th minute, crafting few clear chances. Nevertheless, Carrington, the vice-captain and longest-serving player in Dean Keates’s squad, remains convinced of an imminent improvement. “We have not created a significant number of chances, but that will come,” he stated. “Teams invariably experience such phases during a season; subsequently, one may secure a substantial victory and such periods are swiftly forgotten. I would not be overly concerned—it remains early in the campaign.”

Manager Dean Keates undertook a substantial squad restructuring during the summer. However, Carrington explicitly rejects citing this transition as a justification for the team’s current shortcomings. “It is challenging, but we must adapt rapidly,” he affirmed. “We cannot use that as an excuse. We need to think quickly and resolve the situation.” The match against Dover represented an opportunity to build momentum following a first victory of the season against Maidenhead United. Despite another energetic start, Wrexham had no effective response to Ryan Bird’s early goal. “Our opening fifteen minutes were reasonably good; we applied pressure,” Carrington reflected. “After the goal, we endeavoured to regain a foothold, but it ultimately did not appear to be our day. Dover execute their game plan effectively, advancing the ball quickly and applying sustained pressure. We must now simply regroup for tomorrow’s fixture against Gateshead.”

Analyzing the decisive goal, which resulted from a favourable bounce to Bird within the penalty area, Carrington noted a recurring theme. “It was another fortunate ricochet, similar to Tuesday, presenting him with an opportunity in the box against which defenders can do little. Our imperative is to convert the limited chances we do create, such as the couple we had early in the first half.” He further contextualized the team’s recent performances through the lens of narrow margins. “The first game was inherently goalless, decided by a single chance. Today, again, they scored from essentially one opportunity. Tuesday provided an excellent victory. Currently, the differences are exceedingly fine, but I am confident we will rectify these issues. Once circumstances begin to favour us, we will embark on a positive sequence of results.”

An international Inuit group is angry they weren't informed that a rocket stage likely containing highly toxic fuel is set to splash down in waters they routinely hunt for food.
Okalik Eegeesiak, of the Inuit Circumpolar Commission, said both the federal government and the European Space Agency again failed to inform Inuit in Canada and Greenland about the falling debris.
"Again, we had no knowledge of this and were not included in what is happening in our areas. Our communities are hearing through the media about what is happening."
On Wednesday, a Russian rocket bearing a European environmental monitoring satellite is scheduled to launch. The second stage of the rocket is expected to fall into the waters of Baffin Bay, outside Canada's territorial waters but within its exclusive economic zone as well as the purview of the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act.
The rocket is a repurposed Soviet-era SS-19 ballistic missile, fuelled by hydrazine. Hydrazine is highly carcinogenic and so toxic nearly every space program in the world has moved away from it.
However, the old SS-19s are economically attractive, said Michael Byers, a professor of international law who has studied the issue.
"These are leftover from the Cold War," he said. "They're free as a result."
The second stage of an SS-19 could have as much as a tonne of leftover hydrazine when it hits the waves.
Officials with the agency say the fuel burns up before it hits the Earth. But studies at Russian launch sites have reached different conclusions.
Eegeesiak points out the stage will fall into the North Water Polynya, the most productive and biodiverse place in the Arctic seas. Whales, seals, polar bears and walrus are found there in large numbers and Inuit from both Canada and Greenland hunt frequently there.
rewrite:
The Inuit Circumplar Council has expressed significant concern regarding the lack of consultation and notification about the anticipated splashdown of a rocket stage containing residual hydrazine fuel in marine areas integral to Inuit subsistence hunting. Okalik Eegeesiak, representing the Council, stated that neither the Canadian federal government nor the European Space Agency (ESA) informed Inuit communities in Canada and Greenland about the falling debris, marking a recurring failure in engagement. Eegeesiak emphasized that communities learned of the event through media reports, underscoring their exclusion from discussions concerning activities within their territories.

The incident pertains to the scheduled launch of a Russian rocket carrying an ESA satellite. The rocket's second stage is projected to descend into Baffin Bay. While this area lies beyond Canada's territorial waters, it is within its exclusive economic zone and falls under the jurisdiction of the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act. The launch vehicle is a repurposed Soviet-era SS-19 ballistic missile, which utilizes hydrazine as a propellant. Hydrazine is a recognized carcinogen with high toxicity, leading most global space programs to discontinue its use.

Michael Byers, an international law professor who has examined the issue, notes that the economic incentive for using such rockets is considerable, as they are remnants from the Cold War era and are effectively cost-free. It is estimated that the second stage may contain up to one tonne of unspent hydrazine upon impact. While ESA officials assert that the fuel will combust prior to reaching Earth, independent studies conducted at Russian launch sites have contested this claim.

Eegeesiak further highlighted that the projected impact zone is the North Water Polynya, a region renowned as the most biologically productive and diverse area in the Arctic Ocean. This polynya sustains large populations of whales, seals, polar bears, and walrus, and is a frequent hunting ground for Inuit from both Canada and Greenland, thereby elevating the potential ecological and subsistence risks posed by the debris.

Borderer Elaine Kellington has won household insurance provider HomeProtect’s inaugural landlord of the year award.
Mortgage consultant Elaine, of Kelso, has welcomed more than 30 tenants into her homes since becoming a landlord 10 years ago.
“I feel extremely privileged,” she said.
“I know there are lots of landlords who do a fantastic job, so to be chosen as landlord of the year was such a surprise.
“I pride myself on developing a balanced relationship with tenants, combining business acumen and professionalism with being approachable and setting clear procedures and lines of communication.
“I also believe it’s important to have a flexible mindset and the ability to understand and empathise at times.”
“Getting this award gives me so much gratitude knowing my tenants have taken the time to nominate me and genuinely appreciate all that I do.”
HomeProtect chief executive officer Mark Eastham said: “On behalf of the team, I’d like to say congratulations to our winner, Elaine.
“I’d also like to thank everyone who got involved as the quality of nominations has been phenomenal, with many tenants getting in touch to say just how grateful they are of the outstanding service their landlord provides.
“Our first landlord of the year award was a tremendous success.”
For further details, visit www.landlordawards.com

Roasting conditions and the shadow of Paddy Maguire chasing him around Pairc Sean Mac Diarmada made for a tough afternoon for Conor McManus but one of the country's finest forwards still emerged with a personal tally of five points.
Having patiently signed every autograph and posed for every selfie sought by both Monaghan and Leitrim fans, Conor gave his thoughts on Monaghan's performance and acknowledged it was a difficult afternoon despite the 1-19 to 0-9 scoreline (see report).
“It was tough, we wouldn't be accustomed to that sort of weather for prolonged periods of time in Ireland but it was the same for us as it was for Leitrim.
“It was just about getting off to a fast start and Leitrim put it up to us early on. We were slow to get going but as the game wore on we grew into the game and probably took control towards the end of the half but conditions were tough.”
Leitrim appeared to be a lot more running in the opening stages but Conor insisted it wasn't a deliberate decision to conserve energy.
“It wasn't a tactic, no. You go out and you give it your all from the start and Leitrim were full value for their place in this round of the Championship because they were full of energy and full of life early doors. It took us until later in the game to wear them down.”
A trip to Pairc Sean to face a team they may have been unfamiliar with could have been viewed as a potential banana skin but Conor felt the most important thing from a Monaghan point of view was to focus on their own game.
“It can be tricky but I suppose the key to it is just focusing on yourself and what you can do for you own team.
“There is no point getting caught up too much on the opposition, you just have to focus on your own performance and trying to improve that every day you go out and it is a case of trying to do that more so than anything.”

rewrite:
The challenging meteorological conditions and the persistent defensive efforts of Leitrim's Paddy Maguire rendered the afternoon arduous for Conor McManus at Páirc Seán Mac Diarmada. Nevertheless, the distinguished forward succeeded in registering a personal contribution of five points. Following the match, having diligently accommodated requests for autographs and photographs from supporters of both counties, McManus reflected upon Monaghan’s performance. He acknowledged the inherent difficulties of the contest, notwithstanding the conclusive final scoreline of 1-19 to 0-9.

McManus characterised the conditions as formidable, noting, “It was a demanding encounter. Prolonged periods of such weather are not customary in Ireland, though it was a factor for both teams equally.” He elaborated on the match’s progression, stating, “Initiating the game with momentum was essential, and Leitrim presented a significant challenge from the outset. Our start was somewhat measured, but we gradually established a rhythm as the half advanced, ultimately securing a degree of control by the interval, despite the persistent environmental challenges.”

While Leitrim demonstrated considerable dynamism and a high work rate in the initial phases, McManus refuted the suggestion that Monaghan had adopted a deliberately conservative tactical approach to conserve energy. “It was not a premeditated tactic,” he clarified. “The objective is always to commit fully from the beginning. Leitrim were entirely deserving of their position at this stage of the Championship; they exhibited notable vigour and intensity in the early stages. It required a sustained effort throughout the contest to gradually diminish their resistance.”

Away fixtures against less familiar opposition, such as the visit to Páirc Seán, can present unforeseen pitfalls. McManus, however, emphasised the primacy of internal focus from a Monaghan perspective. “Such fixtures can indeed be precarious,” he conceded. “The crucial element, I believe, is to concentrate on one’s own responsibilities and contributions to the team. Excessive preoccupation with the opposition is counterproductive. The imperative is to focus on personal and collective performance, with the continual aim of enhancement every time one takes the field. That pursuit of improvement is the paramount objective.”

Every once in a while, a movie comes along that is so resoundingly terrible that it achieves perfection. It doesn't just have a lame twist, awful acting, or some kind of cheesy technology. It has everything. And that's exactly the vibe you'll get from Replicas, the astoundingly ridiculous new movie starring Keanu Reeves and the robot from I, Robot.
So here's the plot of Replicas, insofar as one can call it a plot. Reeves is a neuroscientist who has a heads-up display that allows him to teleport (???) his dead wife and children's minds into other bodies (???) or maybe robots (???) or maybe clone them (???). Any movie that earns 12 question marks based on the trailer alone is already destined for cult-classic status.
There are robots that look just like the CGI from I, Robot, which is convenient. Also there is some kind of technology that plunges a needle into your eye, because as I said, this movie has everything. Reeves' lab partner is played by Thomas Middleditch (Silicon Valley), which made me think that at any moment, a crazy VC was going to show up and try to invest in something. A social media platform that stabs your eyes preemptively before you start posting? Sounds great! [Bong hit.]
Replicas' "so bad it's good" bona fides are impeccable. It was directed by Jeffrey Nachmann, who wrote ridiculous fakey-pants climate change movie The Day After Tomorrow (in which Jake Gyllenhaal is chased by "cold" down a hallway). It was written by relative newcomer Chad St. John, whose only other feature credit is a goofy Gerard Butler flick called London Has Fallen, which is about how ONE MAN can prevent EVERY WORLD LEADER from being killed. Plus, as I mentioned earlier, it stars Keanu Reeves. I love me some Keanu, but the guy pretty much specializes in cheesy action flicks.
Even if this movie turns out to be merely bad rather than sublimely horrible, we will always have this trailer. It's the best example I've ever seen of a movie that combines every sci-fi cliché into one intoxicating suicide soda of a plot. Can't wait to watch this one.
rewrite:
Certain cinematic endeavors achieve a paradoxical distinction: they are so profoundly flawed in conception and execution that they transcend mere failure and attain a peculiar form of perfection. This phenomenon is not characterized by a single defective element, such as a contrived narrative twist, deficient performances, or implausible technology, but rather by a comprehensive amalgamation of such shortcomings. It is within this specific paradigm that *Replicas*, a new film starring Keanu Reeves, must be situated. The premise, to the extent it can be delineated, involves Reeves portraying a neuroscientist utilizing a heads-up display to ostensibly transfer the consciousnesses of his deceased family members—through means ambiguously described as teleportation—into alternative vessels, potentially robotic or cloned bodies. A promotional trailer that spontaneously generates a dozen questions regarding basic plot mechanics serves as a preliminary indicator of the film’s destined cult status.

The aesthetic and narrative components further cement this assessment. The robotic designs bear a conspicuous resemblance to the computer-generated imagery of *I, Robot*, while the inclusion of gratuitous technological horror, such as a device that penetrates the ocular sphere, exemplifies the film’s commitment to maximalist absurdity. Casting Thomas Middleditch, known for his role in *Silicon Valley*, as the protagonist’s lab partner inadvertently introduces an aura of tech-industry satire, momentarily suggesting a venture capitalist might appear to fund the very technology depicted. The film’s credentials for being “so bad it’s good” are indeed robust. It is directed by Jeffrey Nachmanoff, co-writer of the scientifically dubious disaster film *The Day After Tomorrow*, and penned by Chad St. John, whose prior major credit is the action film *London Has Fallen*, a narrative predicated on the improbable premise of a single operative thwarting a global assassination plot. The involvement of Keanu Reeves, an actor whose filmography is largely synonymous with a specific genre of stylized action cinema, further aligns with the project’s tonal disposition.

Regardless of whether the final product is ultimately classified as conventionally poor or sublimely terrible, its promotional material stands as a significant artifact. The trailer functions as a masterful compendium of science-fiction clichés, synthesized into a singular, overwhelmingly incoherent narrative concoction. It thereby represents an intriguing case study in the aesthetics of cinematic failure and its unexpected appeal.

April 13 Hong Kong stocks pulled back on Thursday in thin trading as investors were reluctant to stake out positions amid simmering geopolitical tensions.
The benchmark Hang Seng index dropped 0.2 percent, to 24,261.66 points, while the Hong Kong China Enterprises Index was roughly flat at 10,204.34.
Geopolitical risks around the Korean peninsula and the Middle East checked investors' appetite for risk. South Korea said on Thursday it believed it would be consulted by the United States before any possible pre-emptive U.S. strike against Pyongyang.
Markets were also pondering U.S. President Donald Trump's comments to the Wall Street Journal that he preferred interest rates kept low.
On the data from, China reported its overall trade surplus rose in March after logging its first deficit in three years in February.
Most sectors in Hong Kong retreated at the close, with resource stocks leading the decline. An index tracking the sector lost 0.7 percent.
Interest-sensitive property stocks climbed to 6-1/2-month high and gained 0.5 percent at the close. Hong Kong's currency peg to the U.S. dollar ensures that borrowing cost closely follow that of the United States.
China Unicom Hong Kong Ltd was up around 1.9 percent on Thursday, with optimism towards the telecom operator's restructuring reform offsetting its revenue decline in 2016 from the previous year.
(Reporting by Jackie Cai and John Ruwitch; Editing by Shri Navaratnam)
rewrite:
Hong Kong equities experienced a modest retreat on Thursday, April 13, amid subdued trading volumes as geopolitical uncertainties prompted investor caution. The benchmark Hang Seng Index declined by 0.2 percent to close at 24,261.66 points, while the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index remained largely unchanged at 10,204.34 points. Market sentiment was constrained by heightened geopolitical risks, particularly concerning the Korean Peninsula and the Middle East. This cautious stance was reinforced by a statement from South Korea indicating an expectation of prior consultation regarding any potential pre-emptive military action by the United States against North Korea.

Investor deliberation also extended to remarks made by U.S. President Donald Trump, as reported by *The Wall Street Journal*, expressing a preference for maintaining low interest rates. Concurrently, market participants assessed trade data from China, which indicated a return to a surplus in March following a deficit in February—the first in three years.

Sector performance in Hong Kong was predominantly negative by the close, with resource stocks leading the decline, as reflected by a sector-specific index decrease of 0.7 percent. Conversely, interest-sensitive property stocks advanced by 0.5 percent, reaching a six-and-a-half-month high, a movement attributable to Hong Kong's currency peg to the U.S. dollar and its consequent influence on local borrowing costs. Notably, shares of China Unicom Hong Kong Ltd rose approximately 1.9 percent, as positive sentiment regarding the firm's ongoing restructuring efforts mitigated concerns over its reported year-on-year revenue decline for 2016.

MADRID (AP) — Catalonia's fugitive ex-president, Carles Puigdemont, asked the region's parliament on Monday to guarantee his right to attend a session this week in which he hopes to be re-elected government leader, without being arrested.
Spain's Constitutional Court ruled Saturday that Puigdemont, who fled to Belgium following an illegal declaration of independence last October, must be present in parliament to be chosen as the region's chief in Tuesday's session. But a Spanish judge has ordered Puigdemont's arrest on possible rebellion and sedition charges if he re-enters Spain.
The Constitutional Court also said Puigdemont must get court permission to attend the session. Initially, Puigdemont was expected to seek that, but his lawyer said Monday this was unlikely. The lawyer did not rule out Puigdemont's attendance.
The Constitutional Court ruled the session would not be valid if Puigdemont attends without the permit.
Should the Catalan parliament governing board approve Puigdemont's request and encourage his attendance without the permit it would set the chamber on course for further clashes with Spain's government and courts.
Puigdemont is just one of more than a dozen lawmakers and civic group leaders already under investigation for rebellion and sedition relating to an independence push that brought Spain's worst political crisis in decades to a head.
The slim majority regained by separatist lawmakers headed by Puigdemont in Dec. 21 elections has kept the crisis very much alive.
In Tuesday's session, the parliament speaker has two choices. He can ignore the court and allow a vote with Puigdemont present in person, if he turns up, or by video conference, which has been banned by the tribunal.
Alternatively, he can seek another candidate but that would likely outrage the thousands of pro-independence supporters promising to rally outside the chamber.
Polls regularly show most Catalans want the right to decide the region's future, but are evenly divided over splitting from Spain.
rewrite:
On Monday, Carles Puigdemont, the former president of Catalonia currently residing abroad, formally petitioned the regional parliament to ensure his ability to attend an upcoming parliamentary session without facing arrest, wherein he seeks to be reinstated as the head of the regional government. This request follows a ruling issued on Saturday by Spain’s Constitutional Court, which stipulated that Puigdemont must be physically present in the parliament to be eligible for election during Tuesday’s session. Puigdemont has been in Belgium since October, following an unauthorized declaration of independence. However, a Spanish judicial authority has issued an arrest warrant for him on charges of rebellion and sedition, which would be executed upon his re-entry into Spanish territory.

The Constitutional Court further decreed that Puigdemont must obtain judicial authorization to attend the parliamentary session. Although initial indications suggested he would seek such permission, his legal representative stated on Monday that this course of action was now improbable, though Puigdemont’s attendance was not entirely precluded. The court also asserted that any session attended by Puigdemont without the requisite permit would be rendered invalid. Should the parliament’s governing board approve his request and facilitate his attendance absent this authorization, it would precipitate further institutional conflict between the Catalan legislature and the Spanish government and judiciary.

Puigdemont is among more than a dozen political figures and civil society leaders under investigation for rebellion and sedition in connection with the independence movement, which precipitated Spain’s most severe political crisis in decades. The narrow majority secured by separatist parties, led by Puigdemont, in the December 21 elections has sustained this ongoing crisis.

During Tuesday’s session, the parliamentary speaker is confronted with two principal options. The first is to disregard the court’s ruling and permit a vote with Puigdemont participating either in person, should he appear, or via video conference—a method explicitly prohibited by the tribunal. The alternative is to propose an alternative candidate, a move that would likely provoke significant discontent among the numerous pro-independence supporters planning to assemble outside the parliamentary chamber. While opinion polls consistently indicate that a majority of Catalans desire the right to determine the region’s future, public opinion remains sharply divided regarding actual secession from Spain.

Photo: AFP
McDonald’s in France is to offer its customers the slightly more civilized option of eating its best burger with a knife and fork rather than their fingers.
Clients at McDonald’s 1,400 restaurants in France will soon be able to ask for a knife and fork if they don’t fancy eating their burgers with their fingers, Le Figaro reported.
“Cutlery is an evolution, not a break with the past,” said McDonald’s France marketing chief Xavier Royaux.
McDonald’s France announced the revolution after the move was successfully trialed at 10 restaurants in the country.
However knives and forks won’t be given out for an ordinary cheese burger or Big Mac, just for the chain's “signature” gourmet burger – that costs around double the price of other burgers.
The burger giant says the move is to keep up with the competition from restaurants after burger-mania has swept France in recent years.
“For a long time now we have seen a change in the burger market, a multiplication of offers, among these the offers of gourmet burgers, so as a pioneer it is vital we position ourselves, said McDonald’s Royaux.
In recent years the burger has taken over French menus, with some 75 percent of the country’s 145,000 restaurants including it on their menus.
In 2015 some 1.19 billion burgers were sold in France – a rise of 11 percent on the previous year.
Some 80 percent of restaurants say the burger has overtaken steak frites (steak and chips) as the most popular dish among clients.
As well as having to cope with competition from traditional French restaurants, McDonald’s has also had to fend off competition from Burger King, which has returned to France in recent years and the arrival of another US burger giant Five Guys.
In 2015 The Local reported on a survey to show how the burger was rivalling the baguette for French taste buds.
The "jambon beurre" (ham and butter), a staple of the French diet for centuries, was apparently losing ground in the fast-food market to the burger, according to the report by food marketing group Gira Conseil.
rewrite:

According to a report in *Le Figaro*, patrons at the chain's approximately 1,400 French locations will soon be able to request a knife and fork as an alternative to eating with their hands. Xavier Royaux, Marketing Director for McDonald's France, characterized this development as "an evolution, not a break with the past." The initiative follows a successful trial conducted across ten restaurants in the country.

This service, however, will not be extended to all menu items. It will be reserved exclusively for the chain's premium "signature" gourmet burgers, which are priced at roughly twice the cost of standard offerings such as the cheeseburger or Big Mac. The corporation frames this strategic move as a response to intensifying market competition. Royaux explained that the burger market has undergone significant transformation, noting a proliferation of gourmet burger offerings, and stated that as a market pioneer, it is vital for McDonald's to adapt its positioning.

The French culinary landscape has witnessed a notable surge in the popularity of burgers in recent years. Approximately 75 percent of the nation's 145,000 restaurants now feature burgers on their menus. Sales data from 2015 indicates that 1.19 billion burgers were sold in France, representing an 11 percent increase from the previous year. Surveys suggest that for about 80 percent of restaurants, the burger has supplanted the traditional *steak frites* as the most frequently ordered dish.

McDonald's faces competitive pressure not only from traditional French restaurants but also from rival burger chains. Burger King has re-entered the French market, and another U.S. competitor, Five Guys, has established a presence. This competitive dynamic reflects a broader shift in French consumption patterns. A 2015 survey highlighted by *The Local* suggested the burger is rivaling even fundamental elements of French cuisine. A report by the food marketing group Gira Conseil indicated that the classic *jambon-beurre* sandwich, a long-standing dietary staple, is losing ground to burgers within the fast-food market.

WATCH: Last week’s big winter storm may be over, but city officials are still tallying up the costs associated with snow clearing this season. As Calvin To reports, all that salt and sand costs a bundle and it’s still five more weeks until spring.
In Sidney Tuesday, a crew from Garden City Snow and Anti-Ice Services was back to landscaping, building a walkway that would’ve been done last week, had it not been for the snow.
The company converted the majority of its fleet over to spring duty this morning.
It’s a far cry from last week, when heavy snow blanketed parts of Vancouver Island, presenting a major challenge for work crews.
“We have to be ready, which means we move our machines onto site before it snows. We usually do that in the hours leading up to it,” says Colin Eaton, one of Garden City’s owners.
The City of Victoria was one of many places on the island where crews were struggling to keep up with the snow.
“For a few days there, it was enough to keep us busy,” says Ed Robertson, the City of Victoria’s Assistant Director of Public Works.
So far in 2017, the City of Victoria has spent $196,000, much more than the $36,000 in its budget for snow clearing and winter related costs.
The District of Saanich has spent $126,828 out of its $180,000 budget.
The City of Langford pays a private contractor a set fee of $40,000, plus the cost of salt and sand, which has added $20,000 to the cost so far this year.
The City of Nanaimo within its budget, having spent $550,000 out of its total $800,000 budget, which includes a $400,000 reserve.

KENNESAW, Ga. — James Scott hit 5 3-pointers and totalled 30 points as Kennesaw State picked up its second win over USC Upstate in eight days, this time posting a 93-69 rout in the Atlantic Sun Conference rematch on Saturday.
A week ago Anthony Wilson hit the game-winner with 1.4 seconds left for an 81-80 win at Spartanburg.
The Spartans led at intermission, 37-36 after Deion Holmes scored on a layup with :02 left. Mike Cunningham scored at the basket for a 44-43 USC Upstate lead three minutes into the second half, but the Owls responded with a 13-0 run fueled by a Jordan Jones dunk that put Kennesaw State up by 12, 56-44.
Nick Masterson finished with 17 points for the Owls (7-17, 3-6), with Tyler Hooker adding 14.
Cunningham scored 18 points to lead USC Upstate (6-20, 1-8). Ramel Thompkins added 16 and Holmes contributed 12.

Guard James Scott led the effort, scoring 30 points, including five three-pointers. While USC Upstate held a narrow 37-36 halftime lead following a Deion Holmes layup, and later led 44-43 after a Mike Cunningham basket, Kennesaw State seized control with a 13-0 second-half run. This surge was punctuated by a Jordan Jones dunk, establishing a 56-44 advantage. For the Owls (7-17, 3-6), Nick Masterson contributed 17 points and Tyler Hooker added 14. Cunningham led USC Upstate (6-20, 1-8) with 18 points, supported by Ramel Thompkins (16 points) and Holmes (12 points). Oklahoma freshman guard Trae Young is the frontrunner for the player of the year for his jaw-dropping shooting prowess and being seemingly unguardable, regularly taking shots several steps behind the 3-point line.
He’s averaging 30.3 points and 9.5 assists per game going into the Sooners’ matchup Saturday on the road against Texas, and, despite some occasional mistakes — he is still learning, after all — he looks unstoppable in most games.
Young clearly has a bright future, but he’s always looking to get better. One of the things he does — according to a training session filmed by Ballislife.com — is practice taking shots off bad passes because those are obviously going to come from time to time.
Trae Young makes tough shots, because he practices shooting from Bad Passes! #ballislife pic.twitter.com/u4OIKYlkQP — Brad Ballislife (@BradBallisLife) February 2, 2018
More via USA TODAY Sports:
“I love three-pointers,” says Trae Young, Oklahoma’s precocious shooting star — but let’s go a little, uh, deeper. “I thought the further I shot made it cooler, or made it more fun,” he says, referring to when he was first learning the game. “So I always tried to shoot it (from) as far back as I could.”
He is frequently compared with Steph Curry, and the Golden State Warrior and LeBron James have both offered their praise of the freshman phenom.
The full Ballislife.com video is about 19 minutes long and highlights Young’s incredible ball-handling and what drills he repeatedly does to improve his skills. It’s mesmerizing, even for non-game footage.

Entering the Sooners' upcoming road contest against Texas, Young is averaging 30.3 points and 9.5 assists per game. While occasional errors attributable to his ongoing development are evident, his offensive performances have been largely dominant.

Young’s considerable future prospects are matched by a dedicated approach to improvement. As documented in a training session filmed by Ballislife.com, one specific drill involves practicing shots originating from errant passes, preparing for such inevitable in-game situations. This commitment to refining his craft extends to a foundational aspect of his playing style: a profound affinity for long-distance shooting. “I love three-pointers,” Young stated, elaborating that during his formative years, “I thought the further I shot made it cooler, or made it more fun. So I always tried to shoot it as far back as I could.”

The Nigeria Union of Teachers (NUT) has issued a thirty-day ultimatum to nineteen state governments that are indebted to its members for multiple months of salary arrears. Failure to settle these outstanding payments will result in an indefinite industrial action by the union. This declaration was made by the National President of the NUT, Mr. Michael Alogba Olukoya, during a meeting of the union’s National Executive Council (NEC) convened at the Teachers House in Oluyole, Ibadan.

Mr. Olukoya provided a detailed enumeration of the affected states and the extent of their respective salary liabilities. According to his report, Benue State owes ten months of salary, while Ekiti and Cross River States each owe six months. Kogi State, which has reportedly been paying only half-salaries since 2013, currently owes fifteen months. Ondo State owes five months. Further states cited include Taraba, with four months of arrears; Niger, Delta, and Oyo, each owing three months; and Abia, which owes five months. The union leader also highlighted states engaging in partial salary payments: Osun State has paid half-salaries for twenty-three months; Nasarawa for eighteen months; and Plateau State since 2010. Additional states listed are Adamawa (four months), Bayelsa (eight and a half months), and Imo, which is reportedly paying only seventy percent of the monthly salary. Kwara State owes four months, while Borno and Zamfara States have yet to implement the national minimum wage for teachers.

In his statement, Mr. Olukoya explicitly warned, “We hereby give a 30-day ultimatum to all the above-mentioned states to pay all outstanding salaries being owed teachers.” He referenced anticipated disbursements from the Paris Club refunds, expressing the union’s expectation that these funds be utilized to clear the salary backlog. The ultimatum carries a clear consequence: should any state fail to comply within the stipulated period, the NUT will reconvene to issue a formal notice of industrial action. Mr. Olukoya emphasized the seriousness of the situation, stating on behalf of the union’s nationwide membership, “There is going to be total disconnect between us and such governments.” He further clarified the limited participatory role of local government councils in this matter, underscoring the primary fiscal responsibility of the state governments.
