The head of the royal commission into the banking sector has signalled lenders should adhere to a short list of commitments headed by a promise not to mislead consumers in a bid to make life easier for those needing a loan.
Commissioner Kenneth Hayne, after almost a full day of evidence from the head of the Commonwealth Bank’s risk sector, said it appeared “four or five points” could act as a guide for bank officers when dealing with borrowers.
He said a promise not to mislead, to act in a fair manner, deliver loans that were “fit for purpose” with a pledge to responsible lending objectives might cover many of the problems unearthed at commission hearings.
On its third day of examining Bankwest loans to the small-business sector, Commonwealth Bank chief risk officer David Cohen admitted the bank could have handled a loan to pub owners from the central west of NSW much better.
Mr Cohen said though the $1.2 million loan, which had been made by Bankwest before the Commonwealth took over the institution in 2009, had to be wound up, there had been mistakes in the way the owners had been treated by bank staff.
That included failing to tell the owners the results of an investigative audit that backed selling a pub to cover their outstanding loan.
“Community expectations today would require banks have more open and transparent engagement with borrowers in examples such as this,” Mr Cohen said.
He said there was merit in Commissioner Hayne’s proposals, saying “layer upon layer” of new requirements had been put on lending which had obscured the way bank staff should treat customers.
Mr Cohen also revealed the Commonwealth had actively sought to reduce the commercial property exposure of Bankwest.
Bankwest’s exposure to the sector was almost $15 billion soon after its buyout by the Commonwealth but it was reduced to less than $10 billion by 2012.
Mr Cohen said there were some signs the bank had suffered from a shortage of staff in key areas such as compliance and fraud risk.
rewrite:
The chair of the Royal Commission into the banking sector has indicated that financial institutions should adopt a concise set of principles, foremost among them a commitment to avoid misleading consumers, to simplify processes for individuals seeking loans. Following extensive testimony from the Commonwealth Bank’s chief risk officer, Commissioner Kenneth Hayne suggested that a brief list of “four or five points” could serve as a practical framework for banking personnel in customer interactions. He proposed that undertakings to refrain from deception, to conduct dealings equitably, to provide loans which are “fit for purpose,” and to uphold responsible lending standards would address a significant portion of the deficiencies revealed during the Commission’s proceedings.

During the third day of hearings focused on Bankwest’s small-business lending practices, Commonwealth Bank Chief Risk Officer David Cohen conceded that the bank’s handling of a loan to publicans from regional New South Wales was suboptimal. Mr. Cohen acknowledged that, although the $1.2 million loan—originally issued by Bankwest prior to its acquisition by the Commonwealth Bank in 2009—required termination, the treatment of the borrowers by bank staff involved notable errors. These shortcomings included a failure to disclose the findings of an investigative audit which recommended the sale of a public house to settle the outstanding debt. “Contemporary community expectations would necessitate more open and transparent communication between banks and borrowers in such circumstances,” Mr. Cohen stated.

He further expressed support for Commissioner Hayne’s proposed principles, noting that the accumulation of successive regulatory requirements has complicated lending procedures and obscured fundamental standards for customer engagement. Additionally, Mr. Cohen disclosed that the Commonwealth Bank had deliberately pursued a reduction in Bankwest’s commercial property portfolio. Following its acquisition, Bankwest’s exposure to this sector stood at nearly $15 billion, a figure which was systematically reduced to under $10 billion by 2012. Mr. Cohen also indicated there were indications that the bank had experienced resourcing constraints in critical functions, including compliance and fraud risk management.

Rogers Family(DALLAS) — A 100-year-old Dallas, Texas, runner continues to show the world that you are only as old as you feel.
This weekend, Orville Rogers won big at the 2018 USATF Masters Indoor Track and Field Championships in Landover, Maryland.
“How great it feels at the age of 100 to break five new world track records and to bring home the gold,” he told ABC News on Monday.
In the 100 to 104 age category, Rogers set new records in the 60-meter, 200-meter, 400-meter, 800-meter and 1,500-meter events. And, he did it with his family cheering him on every step of the way.
The former World War II veteran was a bomber pilot who later became a commercial pilot. Rogers started running at the age of 50 and began competing in track meets when he turned 90.
Rogers, also the author of “The Running Man,” said he trains every other day and runs three times a week.
Rogers, a widower, has four children, three of whom are still alive; 14 grandchildren; and 11 great-grandchildren.
“We’re a very close family,” he told ABC News. “We take family vacations every summer for 44 years now and we enjoy getting together anywhere.”
In November, Rogers led partygoers as they collectively ran 100 miles at White Rock Lake in Dallas in celebration of his birthday.
“I live life with a capital ‘L,'” he told ABC affiliate WFAA-TV in November.

Orville Rogers, a centenarian resident of Dallas, Texas, exemplifies the principle that physiological age need not dictate capability. At the 2018 USA Track & Field Masters Indoor Championships in Landover, Maryland, Rogers demonstrated this by securing victory and establishing five new world records within the 100-104 age category. His achievements encompassed the 60-meter, 200-meter, 400-meter, 800-meter, and 1,500-meter events, accomplished with familial support in attendance.

A former bomber pilot during World War II who later pursued a career as a commercial aviator, Rogers initiated his running regimen at age fifty. He commenced formal competition at track meets upon reaching ninety years of age. Adhering to a disciplined training schedule, he exercises on alternating days and runs three times weekly. Rogers is also the author of a publication titled *The Running Man*.

His personal life includes four children, three of whom survive him, fourteen grandchildren, and eleven great-grandchildren. Rogers characterizes his family as exceptionally close-knit, noting a forty-four-year tradition of annual summer vacations. In a notable celebration of his centennial year in November, he led a group at Dallas’s White Rock Lake in collectively running one hundred miles. Reflecting on his outlook, Rogers has stated, “I live life with a capital ‘L,’” underscoring a proactive engagement with his pursuits.

The dozen owners of Lamborghini Venenos--an ultra-rare supercar that costs $4 million and up-- will be receiving some bad news via registered mail: Their Italian dream machines are being recalled.
The 12-cylinder, 750-horsepower models that Automobili Lamborghini SpA billed as a “street-legal racing car” are among about 5,900 Aventadors the carmaker will recall worldwide over risks that a fuel system fault could lead to fires, the company said Tuesday.
Included in the recall are the only three Venenos hardtops sold, which carried a price of about $4 million (3 million euros), plus another nine Veneno Roadsters, originally listed at $4.5 million.
About 1,500 Aventadors, which start at around $400,000, also are affected by the recall in the U.S., according to a recall notice posted on the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s website Tuesday.
The ultra-rare Venenos have appreciated in value like works of art since they were built. Lamborghini said in 2013 that it would sell only three copies of the Veneno to customers for 3 million euros apiece, about $4 million at the time. Automobile Magazine reported in March 2016 that one was listed for sale for $11.1 million.
Over-Revving
In a statement, Lamborghini said faults in the Aventador’s evaporative emissions control system could cause fuel vapors to not be treated properly. Combined with "particular maneuvers" such as "engine over-revving at idle," fuel vapors could contact hot gasses and lead to a fire risk, "especially with a not approved aftermarket exhaust system."
With a full fuel tank, "certain driving conditions" could cause gasoline to come into contact with hot exhaust system components, according to NHTSA.
The company says it’s unaware of any driver or passenger injuries tied to the flaw, though a spokeswoman was unable to say whether any fires have been reported in the affected vehicles.
U.S. owners will be notified by registered mail and can schedule a service appointment at a Lamborghini dealer to upgrade the evaporative system, the company said.
rewrite:
Automobili Lamborghini SpA has issued a global safety recall for approximately 5,900 units of its Aventador model, citing a potential fault within the fuel system that presents a fire risk. Among the affected vehicles are the exceptionally rare Lamborghini Veneno variants. The twelve owners of these automobiles, which include the three hardtop coupes originally priced at approximately $4 million (3 million euros) and nine Veneno Roadsters initially listed at $4.5 million, will be formally notified via registered mail. The recall also encompasses roughly 1,500 Aventadors in the United States, a model with a base price beginning around $400,000, according to a notice published on the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) website.

The Veneno models, powered by a 12-cylinder engine producing 750 horsepower and marketed as street-legal racing cars, have undergone significant appreciation in value since their limited production. Lamborghini initially announced in 2013 that only three Veneno coupes would be sold to clients. By March 2016, *Automobile Magazine* reported one example listed for sale at $11.1 million, underscoring their collectible status.

The identified defect resides in the Aventador’s evaporative emissions control system. According to the manufacturer, a malfunction could prevent fuel vapors from being adequately processed. This condition, when combined with specific driving maneuvers such as engine over-revving while idling, may allow fuel vapors to encounter high-temperature gases, thereby creating a fire hazard. This risk is reportedly amplified if a vehicle is equipped with an aftermarket exhaust system not approved by the manufacturer. The NHTSA further notes that, with a full fuel tank, certain driving conditions could result in gasoline contacting hot exhaust components.

Lamborghini states it is currently unaware of any related injuries to drivers or passengers. However, a company spokeswoman could not confirm whether any fires have been reported in the recalled vehicles. In the United States, remediation will involve owners scheduling a service appointment at an authorized dealership to receive an upgrade to the evaporative emissions system.

To mark the occasion, Seven Sharp reporter and reformed smoker Mike Thorpe spoke to Dr Chris Atkinson, an associate professor of oncology at St George’s Cancer Care Centre in Christchurch, to help you kick the habit. "There is a time in every person who smokes' life where they sort of think, 'I don't need to do this, and that's when you need help,'" Dr Atkinson said. Smokers are four times more likely to kick the habit with the help of a healthcare professional, such as a family doctor, a pharmacist, or a helpline.
Dr Atkinson said it's hard to stop "because the addiction is complex".
"There's lots of different types of nicotine - there's lots of different influences that an addict has."
Smoking influences have lessened over the years as the Government tackles the habit, with cigarette ads being taken off the air, and tobacco sponsorship and smoking in bars being banned.
"I'd like to believe it [will happen] but by gosh, we've got a lot of work to do in the next seven years."
The percentage of smokers is currently at 16 per cent - a sharp decline from 33 per cent in 1983.
"700,000 Kiwis have given up and I think they've given up because the message is out there that it hurts people. Tobacco is hurting people."
rewrite:
In commemoration of the occasion, Seven Sharp correspondent and former smoker Mike Thorpe interviewed Dr. Chris Atkinson, an associate professor of oncology at St. George’s Cancer Care Centre in Christchurch, to provide guidance on smoking cessation. Dr. Atkinson observed, “There is a point in every smoker’s life when they consider, ‘I do not need to do this,’ and that is the moment when support is crucial.” Research indicates that smokers are four times more likely to successfully quit with professional assistance from a healthcare provider, such as a general practitioner, pharmacist, or dedicated helpline.

Dr. Atkinson explained that cessation is challenging due to the multifaceted nature of the addiction. “There are numerous forms of nicotine, and addicts are subject to a variety of influences,” he noted. Societal influences promoting smoking have diminished over recent decades through governmental intervention, including the removal of cigarette advertisements from broadcast media and bans on tobacco sponsorship and smoking in bars.

While the prevalence of smoking has declined sharply from 33 percent in 1983 to a current rate of 16 percent, Dr. Atkinson emphasized the ongoing effort required. “I would like to believe further progress is achievable, but we undoubtedly have substantial work ahead in the next seven years,” he stated. He attributed the success of approximately 700,000 New Zealanders in quitting to widespread public awareness of the harms caused by tobacco.

On a party line vote the House passes a $4 trillion budget. It slashes social programs, repealing Obamacare and turning Medicaid into a pile of vouchers.
None of that is actually happening, though. Not yet, anyway.
The way Senate rules work, you need a two-thirds vote to block a filibuster. So as a practical matter who need a two-thirds vote to pass anything controversial.
But one exception is the budget. Budget bills require only a simple majority.
So Republicans want to use this loophole to pass changes to the tax code.
Instead of drafting a tax bill, they'll put the changes inside the budget. But in order to do that they need a budget to pot things inside.
The bill the House passed is the bill in which to insert tax code changes.
Nobody seems to expect the bill to pass the Senate in the form the House passed.
If you're on Medicaid you probably wonder if I can vouch for that.
I'm not a fan of vouchers.
And that's Crisis at a Glance.
Copyright 2017 Hawaii News Now. All rights reserved.
rewrite:
In a vote divided along party lines, the House of Representatives has approved a budget resolution exceeding four trillion dollars. This proposed budget includes substantial reductions to social programs, provisions for repealing the Affordable Care Act, and a restructuring of Medicaid into a system of voucher-based subsidies. However, these measures are not currently enacted and remain prospective.

Senate procedural rules generally require a supermajority of two-thirds to overcome a filibuster, effectively necessitating that threshold for the passage of contentious legislation. A notable exception exists for budget reconciliation bills, which require only a simple majority for approval. Republican legislators intend to utilize this reconciliation process to enact modifications to the federal tax code. Rather than advancing standalone tax legislation, the strategy involves embedding these changes within the budget resolution. Consequently, the House-passed budget serves as the necessary legislative vehicle for such amendments.

It is widely anticipated that the Senate will significantly alter the budget resolution before any final passage. The potential conversion of Medicaid into a voucher program raises considerable policy concerns regarding beneficiary security and healthcare access. This overview summarizes a critical legislative development.

SAN DIEGO (KGTV) - Point Loma neighbors are rallying to save a beloved bike track - a track they've built with their own hands, but no permits. The track on Famosa and Nimitz Boulevards was threatened on Monday.
“I rushed over here as quick as I could,” Darren Miller said. “I stood in front of the tractor and said, “I’m sorry I can't let you keep doing this.”
It’s still unclear who sent the bobcat to level the track. But - the land belongs to the San Diego Housing Commission.
Miller is a parent of two boys and says he started building the track last March after coming across the empty land. He added the jumps and curves, thinking it would become a sort of secret playground.
“I thought myself and a couple of other dads involved would have a small little track that or six or seven kids knew about. I had no idea that this many people loved it,” he said.
Monday night several families showed up for a rally to save the park, expressing their affinity for the neighborhood track.
“This is the most awesome-est place in the world,” eight-year-old Jude Hudson said, “So much fun because there are some bumps and curves.”
Parents agree.
“We don’t want this to go. This a good place to be and to exercise and to keep them off their phones." Jon Erb said. "You got parents that come out here on a daily basis, so you got chaperones down here and keeps them away from drugs.”
When 10News asked what the deal with the empty land was, the San Diego Housing Commission sent the following statement:
“An unauthorized and unpermitted makeshift bike park was set up by unknown individuals on the undeveloped property that is owned by the San Diego Housing Commission (SDHC) at the corner of Famosa and Nimitz Boulevard.
Some of the no trespassing signs placed on the property by SDHC have been removed. Without sufficient insurance, SDHC, a public agency, cannot allow the property to be used as a bike park.
The property is being planned to be developed as affordable housing. We are pleased to be working with the Community Planning Group on the future development of affordable housing at this site.”
rewrite:
In the Point Loma neighborhood of San Diego, residents are mobilizing to preserve an informally constructed bicycle track, which faces imminent removal due to its unauthorized status on public land. The track, located at the intersection of Famosa and Nimitz Boulevards, was subject to a demolition attempt on Monday, prompting immediate community intervention. Darren Miller, a local parent, recounted his efforts to halt the equipment, stating, “I rushed over here as quick as I could. I stood in front of the tractor and said, ‘I’m sorry, I can't let you keep doing this.’” The entity responsible for dispatching the machinery remains unidentified; however, ownership of the parcel is confirmed to reside with the San Diego Housing Commission (SDHC).

Miller, father of two, initiated the track’s construction in March of last year after encountering the vacant lot. He developed the jumps and contours with the intention of creating a discreet recreational space for neighborhood youth. “I envisioned a modest track known only to myself, a few other fathers, and perhaps six or seven children,” Miller explained. “I was unaware of the extensive community appreciation it would garner.” In response to the threat of removal, multiple families assembled for a rally on Monday evening to express their support for the track. Eight-year-old Jude Hudson articulated his enthusiasm, calling it “the most awesome-est place in the world” due to its varied terrain.

Parents present emphasized the track’s value as a communal asset. Jon Erb noted, “We do not wish to see this space eliminated. It provides a constructive venue for physical activity and social interaction, diverting youth from excessive screen time. Parents frequent the location daily, ensuring supervision and fostering an environment that mitigates exposure to negative influences.” When queried regarding the status of the property, the San Diego Housing Commission issued a formal statement clarifying its position. The statement read, in part: “An unauthorized and unpermitted makeshift bike park was established by unknown individuals on undeveloped SDHC-owned property. Some posted ‘no trespassing’ signs have been removed. As a public agency, SDHC cannot permit use of the site as a bike park without adequate insurance coverage. The property is designated for future affordable housing development, and we are collaborating with the Community Planning Group on this initiative.”

The situation underscores a tension between informal community place-making and formal land-use planning, highlighting competing priorities for urban space.

Temperatures hit an icy -5c in Harrogate this morning as Harrogate drivers - and buses - slowed to a crawl in the coldest day of winter so far.
Despite lighter traffic with some schools having already broken up in town for Christmas, the major roads into the town centre were still clogged up as traffic took a cautious approach on icy roads.
The congestion effected buses, too, and The Harrogate Bus Company posted that some of its most popular services - our 1A, 1B and 1C buses - were experiencing delays.
Harrogate temperatures have now risen to 0c but are expected to fall back this afternoon from 4pm.
Overnight temperatures locally tonight into Tuesday will drop to -2C and tomorrow will be another cold day, though, perhaps, a smidgen warmer than of late.
There may have been very minor snow flurries in Harrogate yesterday, Sunday, but the good news for drivers is that snow is not forecast at all this week.
rewrite: Harrogate experienced its coldest winter morning to date, with temperatures dropping to -5°C. Consequently, both private motorists and public transport services were compelled to reduce speed significantly due to hazardous icy conditions. Although traffic volumes were somewhat diminished, owing to the closure of some local schools for the Christmas period, primary routes into the town centre remained congested as drivers exercised extreme caution. This disruption extended to bus services; The Harrogate Bus Company reported notable delays on several of its key routes, specifically the 1A, 1B, and 1C services. While current temperatures have risen to 0°C, a decline is anticipated from 4pm this afternoon. Forecasts indicate overnight lows of -2°C, leading into a persistently cold Tuesday, albeit marginally milder than recent days. Although minor snow flurries occurred on Sunday, no further snowfall is predicted for the coming week, offering some reassurance to road users.

DETROIT (AP) - Kameron Chatman had 21 points with eight rebounds to lead all five Detroit Mercy starters in double-figure scoring in a 74-60 victory over IUPUI on Friday night.
Chatman, who had four assists and three steals, scored 12 points in the first half when Detroit took a 38-28 lead after shooting 52 percent and leading by as many at 18.
The Titans led the entire game and made 8 of 19 3-point tries. Roschon Prince and Josh McFolley added 14 points with McFolley making four of the Titans' 11 steals. DeShawndre Black scored 13 points and Cole Long 12 with seven assists for the Titans (7-17, 3-8 Horizon).
Jaylen Minnett led the Jaguars (7-15, 4-7), who have lost four straight, with four 3-pointers for his 12 points. IUPUI didn't get closer than seven in the second half.
The victory avenged an 81-66 loss at IUPUI on Jan. 16.

rewrite: On Friday evening, the University of Detroit Mercy men's basketball team secured a 74-60 Horizon League victory over IUPUI. The contest was characterized by the balanced offensive contribution of the Titans' starting lineup, each of whom achieved double-digit scoring. Kameron Chatman led all scorers with 21 points, complemented by eight rebounds, four assists, and three steals. His 12 first-half points helped establish a 38-28 halftime advantage, with the Titans shooting 52 percent from the field and leading by as many as eighteen points. Roschon Prince and Josh McFolley each added 14 points, while McFolley contributed four of the team's eleven steals. DeShawndre Black scored 13 points, and Cole Long finished with 12 points and seven assists. For IUPUI, Jaylen Minnett led with 12 points, all from three-pointers. The Jaguars, who have now lost four consecutive games, trailed by no fewer than seven points in the second half. The result avenged Detroit Mercy's 81-66 loss to IUPUI on January 16th.

OTTAWA — The Supreme Court of Canada says records detailing the abuse of former residential school students can eventually be destroyed.
The unanimous high court ruling today brings clarity to an issue that pitted the privacy of victims against the importance of documenting a dark chapter in Canada's relations with Indigenous Peoples.
Students provided accounts of physical, sexual and emotional abuse as part of an independent assessment process to provide compensation — a program that flowed from a major 2006 settlement agreement.
The Supreme Court upheld a lower court ruling that said the material should be destroyed after 15 years, though individuals could agree to have their stories preserved at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation in Winnipeg.
The federal government unsuccessfully argued the documentary record must be fully preserved to ensure what happened at the residential schools is never forgotten.
It said federal laws governing access to information, privacy and archives provide the proper balance for safeguarding the records of historical value while protecting individual privacy and confidentiality.
The Canadian Press
rewrite:
In a unanimous ruling, the Supreme Court of Canada has determined that records containing accounts of abuse from former residential school students may be subject to eventual destruction. This decision resolves a significant legal conflict between the imperative to preserve a historical record of a dark chapter in Canada’s relationship with Indigenous Peoples and the privacy rights of the individual victims. The records in question were generated through an independent assessment process, established under the landmark 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, to adjudicate compensation claims based on personal testimonies of physical, sexual, and emotional abuse.

The Court affirmed a lower court judgment mandating the destruction of these documents after a 15-year retention period, while permitting individuals to consent to the permanent preservation of their testimonies at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation in Winnipeg. The federal government’s position, which argued for complete archival preservation to ensure the events are never forgotten, was not upheld. The Court concluded that existing federal statutes concerning access to information, privacy, and archives strike an appropriate balance between maintaining records of historical significance and protecting personal confidentiality.

WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. officials are blaming the North Korean government for a series of cyberattacks dating to 2009 against media, aerospace, financial sectors and infrastructure in the United States and around the world.
The FBI and the Department of Homeland Security issued a warning this week, saying the cyberattacks were carried out by actors within the North Korean government who are known as “Hidden Cobra.”
“DHS and FBI assess that Hidden Cobra actors will continue to use cyber operations to advance their government’s military and strategic objectives,” the alert said.
U.S. officials are distributing internet addresses to help networks defend against any attacks. The FBI said it has high confidence that the internet addresses are linked to systems infected with Hidden Cobra malware to further exploit networks. The cyberattacks targeted weaknesses in Microsoft Corp. operating systems and Adobe Systems Inc.’s Flash software, which were patched in January and June, respectively.
The joint alert was issued Tuesday, the same day that American student Otto Warmbier, who was released from serving a 15-year sentence in a North Korean prison for participating in alleged acts against the government, arrived in Cincinnati, Ohio.
The U.S. remains in a standoff with North Korea over its nuclear program. The U.S. has issued sanctions, but Pyongyang has not made any move to give up weapons that it says are a deterrent to any invasion. Thousands of U.S. troops are based in neighboring South Korea, and the Demilitarized Zone between the North and South is one of the most heavily fortified borders in the world.

comments
rewrite:
United States authorities have attributed a persistent series of cyber intrusions, originating as early as 2009 and targeting global media, aerospace, financial, and critical infrastructure sectors, to the government of North Korea. In a formal advisory issued this week, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) identified the perpetrators as state-sponsored actors designated “Hidden Cobra.” The alert asserts that these actors will likely continue cyber operations to support Pyongyang’s military and strategic goals.

To mitigate future threats, U.S. agencies are disseminating specific internet protocol addresses associated with systems compromised by Hidden Cobra malware, which is used to infiltrate and exploit networks. The FBI expresses high confidence in this attribution. These cyberattacks historically exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft Corporation operating systems and Adobe Systems Incorporated’s Flash software; these specific vulnerabilities were remediated with patches released in January and June of this year, respectively.

This joint cybersecurity alert was published on Tuesday, coinciding with the return to Cincinnati, Ohio, of American student Otto Warmbier, who had been released from North Korean detention following a 15-year prison sentence for alleged anti-state activities. The cyber allegations emerge within a broader context of protracted diplomatic tension between the United States and North Korea, primarily concerning the latter’s nuclear weapons program. Despite imposed sanctions, Pyongyang maintains its arsenal as a deterrent, refusing to relinquish its weapons. The ongoing military standoff is underscored by the permanent stationing of thousands of U.S. troops in South Korea and the intensely fortified Demilitarized Zone separating the two Koreas.

2017 has been a banner year for cheap flights around the world. In fact, overall prices for long-haul flights fell by seven percent. That’s great if you want to fly to Europe for the first time or finally see Bangkok’s famed street markets.
Over the last year or two airlines like WOWair, Norwegian, and AirAsia have been offering insanely cheap one way flights over the Atlantic for as little as $89 one way. Of course, there’s a big caveat here. Those prices rarely include seat assignments, onboard food or drinks, checked luggage, or even carry on bags. Still, if you’re willing to ride hard and fast over the Atlantic, you can now get there for less than a hundred dollar bill.
Well, 2018 is likely going to be even better. British Airways and Air France are officially getting into the budget airlines game with crazy cheap flights around Europe and competitive long-haul fares between the continents.
Air France launched Joon on December 1st. Their new budget airline is aimed squarely at “hipster millennials” and tech-savvy travelers. They’re already offering flights around Europe for $46 each way from Orly in Paris. By spring, they’ll have flights from Europe to South America and the Indian Ocean (Seychelles) for about $250 each way with plans to tackle the Trans-Atlantic market to the USA by summer.
British Airway’s Level started up last summer and aims at a broader base. They’re targeting millennials, families, and weekend warriors onto their well-fitted flights. They’re already offering flights between Europe and New York, Montreal, Boston, Los Angeles, Oakland, and Buenos Aires for as low as $149 each way.
What these big carriers seem to have caught on to is that there’s more to budget travel than just flights between Europe and America. Both have added South America and Asia to their destinations, opening a whole new world of exploration for budget travelers. And with at least two new airlines throwing their hat in the budget airfare ring, there’s sure to be some interesting price wars on our travel horizons throughout 2018.
🇪🇸 Trendy stroll through #Barcelona with @mglenriquez! What's your next destination? A post shared by JOON (@weflyjoon) on Oct 9, 2017 at 7:12am PDT
(Via Travel + Leisure)
rewrite:
The year 2017 represented a significant period for the global aviation industry, marked by a notable decline in the cost of long-haul air travel. Aggregate data indicates a seven percent reduction in fares, facilitating increased accessibility for travelers aspiring to visit destinations such as Europe or Bangkok's renowned street markets. This trend was largely driven by the expansion of low-cost carriers, including WOW Air, Norwegian, and Air Asia, which offered transatlantic one-way fares as low as eighty-nine dollars. It is important to note, however, that these base fares typically exclude ancillary services such as seat selection, onboard refreshments, and baggage allowance. Nevertheless, these offerings substantially lowered the financial barrier for transatlantic travel.

Current industry developments suggest that 2018 may witness a further intensification of this competitive landscape. Established full-service carriers are now strategically entering the low-cost market segment. Air France launched its subsidiary, Joon, on December 1, 2017, explicitly targeting a demographic of millennials and technologically-oriented travelers. The carrier has initiated intra-European routes from Paris Orly Airport with one-way fares beginning at forty-six dollars. Expansion plans include the introduction of services from Europe to South America and the Indian Ocean, notably the Seychelles, by spring 2018, with projected fares around two hundred and fifty dollars one-way, followed by intended transatlantic routes to the United States by summer.

Similarly, British Airways' low-cost subsidiary, Level, commenced operations in the summer of 2017 with a broader target market, encompassing millennials, families, and leisure travelers. It currently provides transoceanic service between European hubs and several North and South American cities, including New York, Montreal, Boston, Los Angeles, Oakland, and Buenos Aires, with one-way fares starting at one hundred and forty-nine dollars.

A critical insight demonstrated by these major carriers is the recognition that the budget travel market extends beyond the traditional transatlantic corridor. By incorporating destinations in South America and Asia into their low-cost networks, they are significantly expanding the geographical possibilities for cost-conscious travelers. The entry of these well-resourced competitors into the budget airline sector is anticipated to stimulate further fare competition, potentially leading to a wider array of affordable travel options throughout 2018.

New prosecutor in trial for former Lake County coroner Rudd
hello
A new appellate court prosecutor has stepped in to take over the perjury trial of former Lake County Coroner Dr. Thomas Rudd.
Prosecutor Bernard Murray said he does not anticipate having to delay the trial against Rudd, which is scheduled Jan. 16. Judge Victoria Rossetti asked the two sides to return to court Jan. 11 for a hearing on pretrial motions.
Murray took over the case after former prosecutor Brian Towne, 49, was charged with 13 counts of official misconduct and four counts of misapplication of funds stemming from his tenure as state's attorney in LaSalle County. The charges state Towne used public funds for personal use.
Rudd, 70, of Lake Forest, faces five counts of perjury charging him with making false statements on nominating petitions filed prior to an unsuccessful re-election bid in 2016. He faces up to five years in prison if convicted, though probation also is possible.
Authorities say Rudd swore under oath he was present when voters signed his nominating petitions. Prosecutors said 15 to 20 signatures on the petitions turned out to be false.
Rudd remains free on $150,000 bail.
rewrite:
A new appellate court prosecutor has assumed responsibility for the perjury trial of former Lake County Coroner Dr. Thomas Rudd. Prosecutor Bernard Murray indicated he does not anticipate requesting a delay of the trial, which remains scheduled for January 16. Judge Victoria Rossetti has directed both parties to return to court on January 11 for a hearing concerning pending pretrial motions.

Murray’s appointment follows the charging of former prosecutor Brian Towne, 49, with thirteen counts of official misconduct and four counts of misapplication of funds. These charges, related to Towne’s prior tenure as LaSalle County State’s Attorney, allege the misuse of public funds for personal expenses.

Dr. Rudd, 70, of Lake Forest, is charged with five felony counts of perjury. The indictment alleges he made false statements on nominating petitions filed ahead of an unsuccessful 2016 re-election campaign. Prosecutors contend Rudd falsely attested under oath to witnessing voter signatures on these petitions, which allegedly contained between fifteen and twenty fraudulent signatures. If convicted, Rudd could face a maximum sentence of five years imprisonment, though probation remains a potential outcome. He is currently released on $150,000 bail.

Druze residents of Masada village in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights at a Syria independence day rally on April 17, 2017 (AFP Photo/JALAA MAREY)
Masada (AFP) - Hundreds of Druze on the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights marched Monday for Syrian independence day, carrying portraits of President Bashar al-Assad and chanting anti-Israel slogans.
"God save Syria!" they shouted as they rallied in the town of Masada. "Down with the occupation!"
Israeli officials say there are about 20,000 Druze on the strategic plateau seized by the Jewish state from neighbouring Syria in the 1967 Six-Day War.
Israel subsequently annexed the 1,200 square kilometres (460 square miles) of territory in an action never recognised by the international community.
But the vast majority of Golan Druze have retained Syrian nationality.
The civil war which has ravaged their homeland for the past six years is reflected in local divisions, with Masada opponents of the Assad regime refusing to march behind his picture.
But both sides are united in their opposition to the Israeli occupation, residents told AFP.
"We retain our Syrian identity and follow the path of national resistance," said Nasser Ibrahim, one of the organisers of Monday's march.
"With the crisis in Syria, Israel has increased its measures on the Golan," said Assad opponent Ayman Abu Jabal, referring to what he called Israeli-ordered changes to the Golan school curriculum.
Israel and Syria are still officially in a state of war, but Israel says it has no wish to get involved in the fighting.
It does, however, carry out strikes against its Lebanese foe Hezbollah, which fights for Assad in Syria.
Last month, Israel struck what it said were Hezbollah targets in Syria, drawing Syrian anti-aircraft missile fire in the worst flare-up between the two governments since the Syrian civil war began in 2011.

On April 17, 2017, Druze residents of the village of Masada in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights participated in a rally marking Syrian Independence Day. Hundreds of demonstrators marched through the town, carrying portraits of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad and voicing opposition to Israeli control with chants such as "God save Syria!" and "Down with the occupation!" The event highlighted the complex political allegiances within this community. Israeli authorities estimate approximately 20,000 Druze reside on the strategic plateau, which was seized by Israel from Syria during the 1967 Six-Day War. Israel later annexed the 1,200-square-kilometer territory, an act that remains unrecognized by the international community. Despite the annexation, the majority of Golan Druze have maintained their Syrian nationality.

The ongoing Syrian civil war has introduced internal divisions among the local population. In Masada, opponents of the Assad regime refused to march behind his portrait, illustrating these fractures. Nevertheless, residents reported to AFP that both pro- and anti-Assad factions share a unified stance against the Israeli occupation. Nasser Ibrahim, an organizer of the march, stated, "We retain our Syrian identity and follow the path of national resistance." Conversely, Assad opponent Ayman Abu Jabal criticized what he described as Israeli-imposed alterations to the local school curriculum, asserting, "With the crisis in Syria, Israel has increased its measures on the Golan."

Israel and Syria remain officially in a state of war, and Israeli officials have stated they do not seek direct involvement in the Syrian conflict. However, Israel has conducted military strikes in Syria, primarily targeting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which fights in support of the Assad regime. A notable escalation occurred the previous month, when Israeli strikes on alleged Hezbollah positions drew Syrian anti-aircraft missile fire, marking the most severe flare-up between the two states since the Syrian war began in 2011.

I’m a Christian and I believe in a Christian set of principles based on my faith,” Vought stated. “That post, as I stated in the questionnaire to this committee, was to defend my alma mater, Wheaton College, a Christian school that has a statement of faith that includes the centrality of Jesus Christ for Salvation.”
“I understand you are a Christian. But this country is made up of people who are not just — I understand that Christianity is the majority religion, but there are other people who have different religions in this country and around the world,” Bernie fired back.
Vought responded by saying, “As a Christian, I believe that all individuals are made in the image of God and are worthy of dignity and respect regardless of their religious beliefs.”
“I would simply say, Mr. Chairman, that this nominee is really not someone who is really what this country is supposed to be about,” Sanders concluded. “I will vote no.”
rewrite:
During a recent confirmation hearing, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont engaged in a line of questioning that has prompted scrutiny regarding the constitutional prohibition on religious tests for public office. The exchange centered on comments made by Russell Vought, then a nominee for Deputy Director of the Office of Management and Budget, in a 2016 article defending his alma mater, Wheaton College. In that article, Vought articulated a theological perspective consistent with certain Christian doctrines, stating, “Muslims do not simply have a deficient theology. They do not know God because they have rejected Jesus Christ his Son, and they stand condemned.”

Senator Sanders characterized these written statements as “hateful” and “Islamophobic,” asserting they constituted “an insult to over a billion Muslims throughout the world.” He proceeded to inquire whether Vought himself believed the remarks were Islamophobic. Vought defended his article as a defense of Wheaton College’s statement of faith, which affirms the centrality of Jesus Christ for salvation, and clarified his personal beliefs: “I’m a Christian and I believe in a Christian set of principles based on my faith.”

Senator Sanders countered by emphasizing the nation’s religious diversity, noting that while Christianity is the majority religion, the country includes adherents of many faiths. In response, Vought affirmed a commitment to universal dignity, stating, “As a Christian, I believe that all individuals are made in the image of God and are worthy of dignity and respect regardless of their religious beliefs.” Notwithstanding this clarification, Senator Sanders concluded that the nominee’s views were incompatible with national principles, leading him to announce his opposition: “I would simply say, Mr. Chairman, that this nominee is really not someone who is really what this country is supposed to be about. I will vote no.” This dialogue has subsequently fueled debate concerning the boundaries between personal religious conviction, discriminatory speech, and the constitutional qualifications for federal office.

The Kamloops-South Thompson member of the legislature has scheduled three campaign-style events Tuesday stopping in Surrey, Victoria and finishing the day with an event at Thompson Rivers University in his hometown of Kamloops.
An email from former Liberal cabinet minister Peter Fassbender says B.C. needs a fresh vision to keep the province on track and Stone will make a special announcement about the Liberals party's future.

Former Surrey mayor Dianne Watts announced her intentions for the party's top job last month, along with 38-year-old Terrace businesswoman Lucy Sager and five current provincial Liberal politicians, Sam Sullivan, Mike Bernier, Andrew Wilkinson, Mike de Jong and Michael Lee.

The Supreme Court (SC) on Tuesday halted the Quezon City government from implementing a resolution that increases the city’s real property tax rates from 100 percent to 500 percent.
During an en banc session in Baguio City, the high court issued a temporary restraining order halting the implementation of Ordinance No. 2556 (Series of 2016).
The Alliance of Quezon City Homeowners’ Association questioned the ordinance that adjusts the fair market value of lands, houses and other structures.
Named respondents were Quezon City Mayor Herbert Bautista, the City Assessor’s Office and City Treasurer’s Office.
The SC ordered the Quezon City government to file its comment within 10 days from the receipt of the order.
Mayor Herbert Bautista welcomed the court’s ruling but he urged the SC to resolve the case “the soonest possible time.”
“We have yet to receive an official copy of the decision but the Quezon City government welcomes the development. We pray that the SC will resolve the matter the soonest possible time to ensure the smooth operations of the delivery of basic services to its constituents,” he said.
In a separate statement, the city’s Public Affairs’ office said that the city was “compelled” to adjust the fair market values of real properties after the Department of Finance and the Commission on Audit directed the city government to implement the “long-delayed” adjustment as mandated by Section 219 of Republic Act 7160 or the Local Government Code of 1991. Jomar Canlas and Dempsey Reyes
rewrite:
On Tuesday, the Supreme Court issued a provisional order suspending the implementation of a Quezon City ordinance that substantially increases real property tax assessments. During its en banc session in Baguio City, the Court granted a temporary restraining order against Ordinance No. 2556 (Series of 2016), which raises the city's real property tax rates by percentages ranging from 100 to 500. The legal challenge was initiated by the Alliance of Quezon City Homeowners’ Association, which contested the ordinance's adjustment of the fair market values for land, dwellings, and other structures. Named as respondents in the case are Quezon City Mayor Herbert Bautista, the City Assessor’s Office, and the City Treasurer’s Office. The Supreme Court has directed the city government to submit its comment on the matter within ten days of receiving the order.

Mayor Bautista acknowledged the Court's ruling, stating that while an official copy of the decision is pending receipt, the city government welcomes this development. He further expressed hope for an expeditious resolution of the case to ensure the uninterrupted delivery of essential public services. In a separate explanation, the city's Public Affairs Office clarified that the adjustment of property valuations was undertaken in compliance with directives from the Department of Finance and the Commission on Audit. These agencies instructed the city to execute the long-deferred reassessment as required under Section 219 of Republic Act 7160, also known as the Local Government Code of 1991.

SUNRISE, Fla. — Jonathan Huberdeau scored with 7.7 seconds left in the third period to lift the Florida Panthers to a 3-2 victory over the Detroit Red Wings on Saturday night.
Aleksander Barkov and Aaron Ekblad also scored for the Panthers. Harri Sateri made 26 saves for his third straight NHL win. Keith Yandle had two assists.
Danny DeKeyser scored both goals for Detroit and Petr Mrazek stopped 30 shots in his third straight start.
With the score tied at 2, Huberdeau slid a rebound under Mrazek’s pad from inside the crease. The goal was challenged for goalie interference by Detroit but the call stood.
Barkov broke a 1-1 tie with his goal with 6:22 left in the second period. Evgenii Dadanov passed to Barkov in the high slot and Barkov skated in and beat Mrazek on the glove side.
DeKeyser tied it with his second of the game. Sateri blocked a shot and the bouncing puck went off DeKeyser’s skate as he crashed the net and went across the goal line at 3:00 of the third period.
Ekblad’s goal gave the Panthers a 1-0 lead at 3:14 of the first. Ekblad took a pass from Huberdeau in the slot and backhanded the puck off the post and into the net.
DeKeyser tied the score when his shot from the slot went over Sateri’s shoulder on the stick side at 8:51 of the second.
NOTES: Panthers D Alex Petrovic played his 200th NHL game. … Florida F Jamie McGinn returned after missing two games with an upper-body injury. … The Red Wings played their third game in four days. … DeKeyser played his 350th NHL game.
UP NEXT:
Red Wings: Host the Boston Bruins on Tuesday
Panthers: Host the Vancouver Canucks on Tuesday.
rewrite:
On Saturday evening at the BB&T Center in Sunrise, Florida, the Florida Panthers secured a 3-2 victory over the Detroit Red Wings, with the decisive goal occurring in the final moments of regulation. Jonathan Huberdeau scored the game-winning marker with 7.7 seconds remaining in the third period, converting a rebound from within the crease beneath goaltender Petr Mrazek. The Red Wings challenged the play for goaltender interference, but the ruling on the ice was upheld.

The Panthers established an early lead at 3:14 of the first period when defenseman Aaron Ekblad received a pass from Huberdeau in the slot and executed a backhand shot that caromed off the post and into the net. Detroit defenseman Danny DeKeyser equalized at 8:51 of the second period, firing a shot from the slot that passed over goaltender Harri Sateri’s shoulder. Florida regained the advantage at 6:22 of the same period; captain Aleksander Barkov received a pass from Evgenii Dadanov in the high slot, skated in, and scored on Mrazek’s glove side. DeKeyser recorded his second goal of the contest at 3:00 of the third period to tie the game once more, as a blocked shot deflected off his skate and across the goal line during a net-front sequence.

Sateri earned his third consecutive National Hockey League victory with 26 saves, while Mrazek stopped 30 shots in the loss. Panthers defenseman Keith Yandle contributed two assists. In ancillary notes, Florida defenseman Alex Petrovic participated in his 200th NHL game, and forward Jamie McGinn returned from a two-game absence due to an upper-body injury. The contest marked DeKeyser’s 350th career game and concluded a stretch of three games in four days for Detroit. Both teams are scheduled to play next on Tuesday, with the Red Wings hosting the Boston Bruins and the Panthers hosting the Vancouver Canucks.

On May 2, First Solar Inc. disclosed its financial results for the first quarter of 2017. The company reported quarterly net sales of $892 million, a figure that exceeded the Thomson Reuters I/B/E/S consensus revenue estimate of $667.8 million. This increase relative to the preceding quarter was attributed principally to the sale of the Moapa project, which partially offset a decline in third-party module sales. Qantas has no plans to alter its flight schedule to Exmouth, despite mounting evidence planes have been filling up all year, resulting in higher prices and limited travel options for residents and tourists.
The Shire of Exmouth and Exmouth Chamber of Commerce and Industry has been lobbying the national carrier to boost capacity, with chamber president Barry Sullivan stating evidence suggested current services were above 80 per cent capacity.
Shire president Matthew Niikkula said long-term commitment to increased flight capacity would support investment and jobs growth in Exmouth.
“Qantas and Tourism Australia are using the Ningaloo Reef experience to support the campaign to attract visitors to Australia,” he said.
“Providing additional ongoing seating capacity to Exmouth will make sure people can access that experience they are being promised.
“The first step is to have a commitment to additional flights, and to date that has not happened outside ad hoc, short-term measures such as one-off increases during the coming school holidays.”
Mr Niikkula said bigger planes, additional flights or provision of an Exmouth to Broome link would be beneficial.
QANTAS has slashed airfares from Perth to Broome in a bid to get more people heading to WA's north instead of Bali. The West Australian Video QANTAS has slashed airfares from Perth to Broome in a bid to get more people heading to WA's north instead of Bali.
Qantas refused to confirm the capacity of flights to and from Exmouth, claiming the average amount of people on a plane was commercially sensitive information.
“We currently have no plans to change our schedule for flights to Learmonth, however we are always reviewing our network to ensure that we have the right aircraft on the right route to match demand,” a spokeswoman said.
North West Central MLA Vince Catania said the State Government needed to push airlines to be more honest with the public.
“The Government should be demanding Qantas puts on extra flights as a requirement of their licence,” he said.
“Airlines look at load factor and how they can maximise profits to benefit them, rather than looking at capacity for the community.
“This is not just about reducing airfares, it is about the company being open and transparent on how they come up with their ticket price.”
Mr Catania said Exmouth fares should be capped at $150.
rewrite:
The national carrier, Qantas, has indicated that it intends to maintain its current flight schedule to Exmouth, notwithstanding accumulating data indicating sustained high passenger loads throughout the year. This situation has contributed to elevated airfares and constrained travel options for both local residents and visitors to the region. Local advocacy bodies, namely the Shire of Exmouth and the Exmouth Chamber of Commerce and Industry, have been actively petitioning the airline to augment its capacity. Chamber President Barry Sullivan has cited evidence suggesting that existing services are consistently operating above eighty percent capacity.

Shire President Matthew Niikkula has emphasised that a long-term commitment to increased flight capacity is crucial for underpinning investment and fostering employment growth within Exmouth. He further noted that the destination's primary attraction, the Ningaloo Reef experience, is being utilised by Qantas and Tourism Australia in promotional campaigns to attract international visitors to Australia. "Providing additional, sustained seating capacity to Exmouth is essential to ensure that potential visitors can realistically access the experience being marketed to them," Mr. Niikkula stated. "The fundamental prerequisite is a firm commitment to additional flights. To date, such a commitment has not been forthcoming, beyond transient, short-term measures such as isolated capacity increases during peak periods like the approaching school holidays." He suggested that solutions could involve deploying larger aircraft, adding more frequent services, or establishing a direct air link between Exmouth and Broome.

In response to inquiries, Qantas declined to disclose specific load factors for the Exmouth route, asserting that average passenger numbers constitute commercially sensitive information. A company spokeswoman stated, "We currently have no plans to alter our schedule for flights to Learmonth [Exmouth's airport]. However, we continually review our network to ensure we deploy appropriate aircraft on each route to align with demand." This position has drawn criticism from North West Central MLA Vince Catania, who contends that the State Government should compel airlines to adopt greater transparency with the public. "The Government should mandate Qantas to provide extra flights as a condition of its operating licence," Mr. Catania asserted. He argued that airline decisions are predominantly driven by load factors and profit maximisation, rather than by considerations of community capacity needs. "This issue extends beyond merely reducing airfares; it is fundamentally about corporate transparency regarding the methodology behind ticket pricing," he concluded, proposing that Exmouth fares should be capped at approximately $150.

The iconic “Hollywood” sign got a New Year’s Day makeover from an unknown vandal who used a black tarp to transform the letters into a message celebrating marijuana.
Multiple social media images showed the new “Hollyweed” sign on Mount Lee overlooking Los Angeles. One of the black tarps appeared to have an image of a peace symbol and the other a heart.
Cops have surveillance video of the suspect, TMZ reported. The vandal, dressed in all black, could face a misdemeanor trespassing charge, said Sgt. Robert Payan. The person scaled a protective fence surrounding the sign and then clambered up each giant letter to drape the coverings, Payan said.
California in November passed a measure legalizing marijuana for recreational use.
Though the Prop 64 vote may have been an impetus to change the sign, it wouldn’t be the first time someone has taken to the hills to alter the letters in honor of cannabis. A vandal also changed the sign to read “Hollyweed” on New Year’s Day 1976, TMZ reported.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
rewrite: On New Year's Day, the iconic "Hollywood" sign underwent an unauthorized alteration by an unidentified individual, who employed black tarpaulins to modify the letters into a message endorsing cannabis, resulting in the display "Hollyweed." Photographic evidence disseminated via social media depicted the altered sign situated on Mount Lee, overlooking Los Angeles. The coverings reportedly featured symbols of a peace sign and a heart. According to a report by TMZ, law enforcement officials possess surveillance footage of a suspect clad entirely in black. Sergeant Robert Payan indicated that the individual, who scaled the protective perimeter fence and ascended each letter to affix the materials, could face misdemeanor trespassing charges. This incident follows the passage of Proposition 64 in November, which legalized recreational marijuana in California. While this electoral outcome may have served as impetus for the act, it is not unprecedented; a similar alteration to "Hollyweed" occurred on New Year's Day in 1976, as also documented by TMZ. This account incorporates information from The Associated Press.

Upon entry, deputies encountered eighteen cats and nine dogs cohabitating with the woman and her adult daughter. The elderly woman was found on the floor, surrounded by animal feces. Deputies noted the odor within the home was so severe that masks were required for entry.
Deputy Chris Eaton stated, "I can honestly say the condition of the home was the worst I have ever seen. The floors and the walls were covered with animal feces."
Social Services has initiated an investigation, indicating the daughter may face charges of neglect.
Authorities reported that the animals were in satisfactory physical condition, describing the situation as tragic and noting that the care of the pets appeared to have been prioritized over the human inhabitants.

Rep. Tim Murphy (R-PA), who announced his resignation from Congress Thursday, reportedly ran a office rife with the mistreatment of staffers.
Before his resignation, the vocally pro-life Pennsylvania Republican was revealed to have asked a mistress to get an abortion.
Politico reported the behavior on Thursday, following Murphy’s announcement of his resignation. The outlet reported that a potential investigation into Murphy’s treatment of his employees by the House Ethics Committee motivated his resignation as much as the revelations about his mistress.
Multiple unnamed former Murphy staffers told Politico that the behavior of the congressman’s chief of staff, Susan Mosychuk, had moved them to quit.
“It was one of the worst places I have ever worked in my life. There was screaming. Intimidation. Nothing you ever did was right,” a former Murphy district director, Nick Rodondo, told Pittsburgh radio station KDKA, Politico noted.
Every other source was unnamed: Politico reported that Mosychuk called staffers “worthless” and their work “garbage.”
“It’s not like a private company where you have an HR department,” one former staffer told Politico. “It was a culture of abuse and a culture of corruption. There really is no oversight.”
“Screaming was an everyday thing,” said another unnamed former staffer. “The manipulation and the mind games. … Everybody in that office was depressed.”
Multiple unnamed ex-staffers told the publication the chief of staff used white noise machines placed around the congressman’s office in order to mask the sound of her screaming. Staffers were told to take the stairs instead of the elevator as a punishment, according to one former employee, and bathroom breaks were cut short in order to administer verbal disciplining.
Politico also reported that a leaked June 2017 memo by Mosychuk, called “Office Conduct and Behavior: Harassment/Legal Compliance” and outlining supposed abusive behavior by the congressman, more accurately described Mosychuk’s own behavior.
“She was the one who would verbally abuse staff,” one unnamed ex-staffer said. “He was bad, but you can deal with a tough member. She was literally terrorizing people.”
Read Politico’s full story here.

Lucy Durack on set, on her first day of filming Lift
Lucy Durack on set, on her first day of filming Lift Picture: Ian Munro
It was an odd encounter in the lift at her daughter’s day care that led Lucy Durack home to Perth — and to her debut as a screenwriter.
Durack, an acclaimed theatre actress, will spend much of this week inside a makeshift wooden elevator inside a small film studio in Maylands, shooting Lift, a romantic comedy web series she created and wrote.
Sydney-based Durack, best known for her award-winning turns as Glinda the Good Witch in Wicked and Elle Woods in Legally Blonde: The Musical, said seeing her script come to life was “incredibly, overwhelmingly fun”.
Durack penned five comedies with her writing partners, brother and sister duo Jess and Leon Murray, but they settled on Lift partly because of its format of seven four-minute episodes.
The story follows Olivia (Durack) on her way to a job interview and Simon (theatre actor Duncan Ragg), who is about to propose to his girlfriend, and their fateful meeting in an elevator.
“I love a romantic comedy ... and this one came out of a fairly awkward conversation I had with a stranger in a lift at my daughter’s day care,” Durack laughed.
Actress and singer Lucy Durack is back home in Perth visiting her family for a week. She is also appearing in new Nine series Doctor Doctor. Picture: Ian Munro
“We wanted something we could make on a small budget, before we got funding from Screenwest.
“The rules were each episode was one lift ride and there was one location, so we had to stretch the boundaries to make it into a real romantic comedy, just in microscopic form.”
And when Lift goes online midyear, it will be the culmination of tireless work by “an incredible team of up-and-coming WA crew and volunteers”, according to producer Lauren Elliott.
WA’s Zoe Pepper is directing and Chloe Rickard is executive producer. As Durack points out, it is an all-female line-up at the helm. “It’s just cool to be on a set with so many women,” she said. “It’s really inspiring and exciting.”

CHARLOTTE, North Carolina, Aug 12 (Reuters) - Hideki Matsuyama has broad shoulders but is not finding it easy to carry the weight of an entire nation as he seeks to become the first Japanese man to win a major.
Matsuyama started the third round of the PGA Championship tied for the lead with Kevin Kisner but never got into gear, a bogey at the first setting the table for a pedestrian one-over-par 72.
That was still good enough to remain in contention, a stroke behind Kisner, who dropped three shots in the final three holes.
"Probably the pressure had something to do with it, being in the last group in a major tournament," said Matsuyama.
"But I haven't been spot-on all week, and the worries I had about my swing showed up today in the way I played.
"I'm disappointed the way I played today, however I'm happy to be one stroke back and still have a chance and looking forward to tomorrow."
Matsuyama is coming off a closing 61 that clinched a runaway victory at last week's WGC-Bridgestone Invitational. He said at the time he had shot the stunning score despite being uncomfortable with his swing, words he repeated pre-tournament here.
Despite his struggles, the 25-year-old played the difficult final three holes better than his rivals, parring them all to finish the day much closer than he expected an hour previously.

An initial bogey precipitated a subdued performance, resulting in a one-over-par 72.

Nevertheless, this score maintained his competitive position, leaving him one stroke behind Kisner, who conceded three shots over the final three holes. Matsuyama attributed aspects of his performance to the pressures of contention. "The pressure likely contributed, given my position in the final group of a major," he stated. "My play has not been precise throughout the week, and existing concerns regarding my swing manifested in today's execution. While disappointed with today's performance, I remain satisfied to be within one stroke and retain an opportunity, anticipating tomorrow's round."

This follows a final-round 61 that secured a decisive victory at the preceding week's WGC-Bridgestone Invitational. Matsuyama had previously noted achieving that score despite swing discomfort, a sentiment he reiterated prior to this tournament. Despite today's challenges, the 25-year-old navigated the demanding final three holes more effectively than his competitors, recording pars on each to conclude the day in closer contention than anticipated.

During CBS’ coverage of the shooting at a Congressional baseball practice, anchor Charlie Rose stated, “people talk about things like ‘lock her up,’ and we saw some of the most crude political language that we’d heard. … This has been a season of sort of coarse political rhetoric.”
Rose said, “[W]e saw during the time that members went back home, because of some of the debates in Congress, they were particularly raucous town meetings, not about threats to their lives, but clearly, the level in combativeness was more apparent than ever.”
He later added, after Congressional Correspondent Nancy Cordes said that it can be difficult for members of Congress to tell who is merely exercising their free speech rights and someone who has the intent of committing violence, “Clearly, we saw that during the campaign, which people talk about things like ‘lock her up,’ and we saw some of the most crude political language that we’d heard, even though there’s a long history of political attacks in American politics since the Founding Fathers. We did see expressions that we had not heard before. This has been a season of sort of coarse political rhetoric.”

After Desrosiers’ trey, Yale missed consecutive 3-point shots and fouled Amir Bell, who missed the front end of a one-and-one. The teams exchanged turnovers before a desperation 3-point try by Yale missed.

DAYTON, Ohio (WDTN) – A local attorney is warning that we could begin to see more violent crimes taking place on social media.
Following Sunday’s live broadcast on Facebook of a deadly shooting in Cleveland he’s concerned about the direction social media is headed.
Cyberspace attorney, Andrew Rossow says social media plays a major role in how suspects are traced and prosecuted. He says what happened on Facebook Live in Cleveland is disturbing, but may just be the beginning.
“People are starting to live through their devices and online technology. Hiding behind their Facebook user names or Twitter handles, thinking people can’t find them,” said Rossow with the Gregory M. Gantt Co., L.P.A law firm.
He says if you see a crime on social media, call law enforcement immediately. Also, if you think what you’re posting is private, it’s not. He says Facebook’s policy allows posts to be traced if requested through the legal system.
“You hope people understand right from wrong, but some people don’t and unfortunately, the next thing is going to be what is the next thing that’s going to happen,” he said.

This concern follows the live broadcast of a fatal shooting in Cleveland on Facebook this past Sunday. Attorney Andrew Rossow, who specializes in cyber law, emphasizes the significant role social media now plays in the identification and prosecution of suspects. He characterizes the Cleveland incident as deeply troubling and potentially indicative of a broader trend. Rossow, of the Gregory M. Gantt Co., L.P.A., observes that individuals are increasingly conducting their lives through digital devices and online personas, often operating under a false sense of anonymity afforded by usernames and handles. He advises the public to contact law enforcement immediately upon witnessing criminal activity on these platforms. Furthermore, he stresses that users should not assume their posts are private, noting that Facebook’s policies permit data to be traced through proper legal channels. Rossow concludes by expressing a hope for public discernment, while acknowledging the unpredictable and potentially escalating nature of such online behaviors.

Students take part in a protest to demand the appearance of three missing film students alive, in Guadalajara, Jalisco state, Mexico, on March 24, 2018. Three film students from the University of Audiovisual Media of Jalisco state went missing March 19.
Authorities said Monday that three Mexican film students who went missing in March in Guadalajara were kidnapped, tortured and killed, and their bodies were dissolved in acid, NBC News reported.
Javier Salomón Aceves Gastélum, Daniel Díaz, and Marco Ávalo were last seen on March 19 in the municipality of Tonala, in the state of Jalisco, filming a class project during their Spring Break. The three aspiring filmmakers were students at the Universidad de Medios Audiovisuales.
According to state prosecutors, their car broke down during the trip and they were later kidnapped by gunmen from the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), who confused them for members of a rival gang.
Academy Award winning director Guillermo del Toro, who is a native of Guadalajara, expressed outrage on social media in response to the killings.
"Words can't explain the dimension of this madness. 3 students are killed and dissolved in acid. The "why" is unthinkable, the "how" is terrifying,” the "Shape of Water" director tweeted.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A research team from Taipei City University of Science and Technology won one gold award and three special prizes for their smart baby carrier at a trade show in Goyang, South Korea from June 27-July 1, reported CNA.
The smart baby carrier has self-regulated heating, sensors to ensure the baby is strapped in safely and Bluetooth functionality to help caregivers take better care of the child.
The research team attended the Korea International Women's Invention Exposition 2018 and walked away with multiple awards.
The successful research team is an interdisciplinary group of computer scientists and communications engineers, and was comprised of both students and teachers.
Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer and Communication Engineering, Taipei City University of Science and Technology Tsai Yao-pin (蔡耀斌) said baby carriers are a very important product and none available to buy have heating capability.
This gap in the market led the research team to develop their award winning invention, Tsai said.
Research team member and third year student Chen Wei-hung (陳威宏) said the team added a warming pouch to keep the baby's bottle warm at about 45 degrees Celsius.
An infant is unlikely to drink cold milk, he added.
The baby carrier has Bluetooth functionality, allowing it to link to a smart phone to display temperature information to help caregivers to take better care of child, Chen said.
Tsai said that most parents fret about whether the baby carrier is buckled and fastened correctly. In response, their invention had a sensor installed which illuminates if the baby carrier is fastened incorrectly.
The research team is currently in discussions with manufacturers from Hong Kong and Taiwan about bringing the award-winning invention to market.
rewrite:
A research team from Taipei City University of Science and Technology garnered one gold award and three special prizes at the Korea International Women's Invention Exposition, held in Goyang, South Korea, from June 27 to July 1, 2018. Their entry, an innovative smart baby carrier, was recognized for its integrated functionalities designed to enhance infant care. The device incorporates self-regulating heating elements, safety sensors to verify correct securement, and Bluetooth connectivity for remote monitoring.

The interdisciplinary team, composed of both faculty and students from computer science and communications engineering disciplines, identified a market deficiency in existing baby carrier products. As noted by Assistant Professor Tsai Yao-pin of the Department of Computer and Communication Engineering, commercially available carriers lack integrated heating capabilities, a feature the team sought to address. This perceived gap motivated the development project.

Team member Chen Wei-hung, a third-year student, elaborated on the design specifics. The carrier includes a warming pouch capable of maintaining an infant's bottle at approximately 45 degrees Celsius, a temperature deemed suitable for consumption and intended to prevent the refusal of cold milk. Furthermore, the Bluetooth module transmits real-time temperature data to a paired smartphone application, providing caregivers with continuous oversight. Addressing prevalent parental concerns regarding proper fastening, the team integrated a sensor mechanism that provides visual confirmation—illuminating if the carrier is incorrectly fastened—thereby promoting safety.

The project has progressed beyond the prototype stage, with the research team currently engaged in preliminary discussions with potential manufacturers in Hong Kong and Taiwan to explore commercial production and market distribution of the award-winning invention.
