rewrite:
The extent to which professional attire influences workplace productivity and success remains a subject of inquiry. This raises several questions: might the formal business attire an individual dons daily contribute to their professional drive and achievements? Conversely, could a habitual wardrobe consisting of jeans and polo shirts inadvertently hinder performance? Alternatively, is it possible that sartorial choices bear no substantive relationship to work output?

Vishal Agarwal, former managing director at GE, explores these questions in his recent publication, *Give to Get: A Senior Leader’s Guide to Navigating Corporate Life*. He posits that the productivity of employees who adopt a predominantly casual style may be, in effect, "taking a vacation," and contends that even professionals in technical fields should consider "dressing for success." In an interview with Mike Doria, Agarwal elaborated that in roles where formal attire is the established norm—such as in law, executive leadership, investment banking, corporate management, and consulting—maintaining sartorial standards is critical. He argues that consistent formal dress enables professionals to perform optimally, maintain commercial intensity, and sustain momentum, suggesting that casual attire in such environments can impede productivity.

Agarwal acknowledges that attire should align with corporate brand identity; if a company’s brand permits a casual dress code, adherence to that specific standard is acceptable. However, he distinguishes between business casual and a sloppy appearance, noting that unkempt clothing or lack of grooming does not constitute appropriate business casual attire. While the four general categories of workwear may overlap, Agarwal indicates that an organization’s official handbook should provide definitive guidance. Despite his observations, Agarwal notes that throughout his leadership career he has encountered no empirical data, only anecdotal evidence, to suggest that casually attired employees demonstrate incrementally greater output.

Fighters and team members prepare backstage before matches of a Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) competition in Kabul, Afghanistan March 30, 2017. REUTERS/Omar Sobhani
An Afghan athlete is checked before a mixed martial arts (MMA) match in Kabul, Afghanistan March 30, 2017. REUTERS/Omar Sobhani

An Afghan fighter in knockout in the ring during a mixed martial arts (MMA) match in Kabul, Afghanistan March 30, 2017. REUTERS/Omar Sobhani
KABUL In a custom-built arena in Kabul, crowds cheered as young Afghan men punched, kicked, and wrestled in the country's first professional mixed martial arts league, a welcome distraction to the violence besetting the country.
While cricket and football more commonly grab public attention in Afghanistan, fighters and fans see martial arts not just as entertainment but as a constructive pastime for youths in a country torn by war and economic malaise.
Against a soundtrack of booming music and shouts of encouragement, sweat and blood mixed inside the cage. Each match, however, ended in a hug.
"I think it provides a very good platform for the social frustrations that we have here in Afghanistan," said Kakal Noristani, who a year and a half ago helped found the Snow Leopard Fighting Championship.
To date, only men have competed in the handful of competitions, but organizers say they are training women fighters. The walls of the club feature posters of American martial arts competitor Ronda Rousey.
Noristani and his partners want to develop mixed martial arts as a professional sport in Afghanistan, hoping to host foreign fighters and send Afghan competitors abroad.
"We’ve just begun here in Afghanistan," Noristani said. "The professional structure was non-existent before this."
That's helped some fighters dream of national and international glory.
"This is the wish of every fighter: To reach the highest level and be able to fight abroad," said Mir Baba Nadery, who won his match that night.
Outside the cage, spectators expressed gratitude for a diversion from the country's woes.
"Coming to these kind of events takes your mind off of our problems," said Nadia Sina. "We are happy to see such an organization encouraging sportsmen and improving the sport in the country."
(Writing by Josh Smith; editing by Richard Lough)

To date, participation has been exclusively male across the limited number of events held. However, organizers indicate that female fighters are currently in training, a point underscored by the presence of promotional imagery featuring American martial artist Ronda Rousey within the facility. Noristani and his associates aim to cultivate MMA as a professional sport within Afghanistan, with aspirations to both host international fighters and facilitate opportunities for Afghan athletes to compete overseas. After thrilling more than 8 million people worldwide, CORTEO will visit Chattanooga at the McKenzie Arena for a limited run of six performances, from May 10 to 13, 2018.
This unique production directed by Daniele Finzi Pasca premiered in Montreal in April 2005 and has visited 64 cities in 19 countries.
CORTEO, which means cortege in Italian, is a joyous procession, a festive parade imagined by a clown. The show brings together the passion of the actor with the grace and power of the acrobat to plunge the audience into a theatrical world of fun, comedy and spontaneity situated in a mysterious space between heaven and earth.
The clown pictures his own funeral taking place in a carnival atmosphere, watched over by quietly caring angels. Juxtaposing the large with the small, the ridiculous with the tragic and the magic of perfection with the charm of imperfection, the show highlights the strength and fragility of the clown, as well as his wisdom and kindness, to illustrate the portion of humanity that is within each of us. The music turns lyrical and playful carrying CORTEO through a timeless celebration in which illusion teases reality.
The cast of CORTEO includes 51 acrobats, musicians, singers and actors from all around the world.

BLOEMFONTEIN, South Africa — South Africa openers Aiden Markram and Dean Elgar both made centuries to punish Bangladesh's decision to bowl first in the second test on Friday.
Markram was 135 not out and Elgar fell for 113 to break their 243-run stand for the opening wicket. South Africa moved to 256-1 at tea on the opening day at Mangaung Oval in what was shaping up to be a repeat of the first test.
Then, Bangladesh misread the pitch, put South Africa in to bat, and the South Africans made 496-3 declared in their first innings on the way to a comfortable victory.
Elgar made a second century in two tests after his 199 in that big first-innings score in the first game. Markram, out for 97 on his debut in the first test, did complete a maiden test hundred this time in Bloemfontein.
He had hit 21 fours and was with Hashim Amla (1 not out) at the tea break. South Africa was moving along swiftly at over 4 1/2 runs an over.
Elgar now has five centuries in 2017 and is the leading scorer in test cricket this year. He and Markram have put on two big opening partnerships in their first two tests playing together, 196 in the opening game and the double-century stand on Friday.
Elgar fell to a short-ball tactic that Bangladesh persevered with through most of the day, and ultimately had success with. Subashis Roy banged in a short one, Elgar went for a hook, and was caught at backward square leg by Mustafizur Rahman.
The touring bowlers reverted to the short stuff after getting little out of the pitch early on. They were also wayward, conceding 38 boundaries in the first two sessions.
Bangladesh made four changes to its lineup for the second and final match, dropping three bowlers and bringing in Subashis, Rubel Hossain and Taijul Islam. South Africa was without injured strike bowler Morne Morkel. Wayne Parnell replaced him.
By The Associated Press
rewrite:
In the second Test match held at Mangaung Oval in Bloemfontein, South Africa, the decision by Bangladesh to field first after winning the toss proved disadvantageous, as South African openers Aiden Markram and Dean Elgar each scored centuries. At the tea interval on the first day, South Africa had reached 256 for one, largely due to a 243-run opening partnership. Markram remained unbeaten on 135, while Elgar was dismissed for 113. This strong beginning echoed the pattern of the first Test, wherein Bangladesh similarly misjudged the pitch conditions, opted to bowl, and subsequently conceded a first-innings total of 496 for three declared, leading to a comprehensive defeat for the touring side.

Elgar’s century marked his second in consecutive matches, following a score of 199 in the initial Test. Markram, having been dismissed for 97 on his debut in the first Test, achieved his maiden Test hundred in this encounter. His innings included 21 boundaries, and at the break, he was accompanied by Hashim Amla, who was one not out. The scoring rate exceeded 4.5 runs per over, reflecting the hosts’ dominant position.

Elgar has now recorded five centuries in 2017, establishing him as the leading run-scorer in Test cricket this year. Furthermore, his partnership with Markram has yielded substantial opening stands in both Tests they have played together: 196 in the first match and a double-century partnership in the second. Elgar’s dismissal resulted from a sustained short-ball strategy employed by Bangladesh, which ultimately succeeded when Subashis Roy delivered a bouncer that Elgar hooked to backward square leg, where Mustafizur Rahman completed the catch.

Failing to extract significant movement from the pitch, Bangladesh’s bowlers relied heavily on short deliveries and struggled with line and length, conceding 38 boundaries in the first two sessions. For this final match of the series, Bangladesh made four changes to their lineup, including the introduction of bowlers Subashis Roy, Rubel Hossain, and Taijul Islam. South Africa, meanwhile, was without the injured Morne Morkel, with Wayne Parnell named as his replacement.

HEMPSTEAD, N.Y. — Grant Riller scored 24 points, Jarrell Brantley poured in 23 more, including the winning layup, and Charleston edged Hofstra 86-85 on Saturday night to take sole possession of first place in the Colonial Athletic Association.
Trailing by a point after Hofstra’s Justin Wright-Foreman sank a 3-pointer with 18 seconds left, Charleston (18-6, 9-3) took the ball down the right side of the court and got it inside to Brantley, who dribbled twice to his right before breaking left to drop in the winning bucket with three seconds remaining.
Joe Chealey added 19 points and Nick Harris had 10 for Charleston, which shot 57 per cent and got 18 assists on its 30 baskets to pick up its sixth straight win.
Wright-Foreman finished with 24 points to lead Hofstra (14-10, 7-5), Eli Pemberton added 20, Jalen Ray got 11 and Kenny Wormley 10.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has again upped its forecast for global growth this year due to buoyant financial markets and a cyclical recovery in manufacturing and trade.
The Washington-based organisation’s forecast rose from 3.1 per cent last year to 3.4 per cent in January. In its latest World Economic Outlook, published on Tuesday, it said it nows sees global growth rising 3.5 per cent in 2017.
The body kept it projection for 2018 unchanged at 3.6 per cent.
However, while highlighting a number of positive developments the body warned that binding structural impediments continue to hold back a stronger recovery with “a balance of risks that remains tilted to the downside, especially over the medium term.”
“Structural problems- such as low productivity growth and high income inequality - are likely to persist. Inward-looking policies threaten global economic integration and the cooperative global economic order, which have served the world economy, especially emerging market and developing economies, well,” the IMF said in its latest World Economic Outlook.
The IMF revised Britain’s growth forecast to 2 per cent for 2017, up a half percentage point from January. It said negative effects from the UK’s vote to leave the European Union are taking longer to materialise.
The organisation held its 2017 US growth forecast steady at 2.3 per cent, which still represents a substantial jump from 1.6 per cent growth in 2016, partly due to expectations that president Donald Trump will cut taxes and increase government spending.
The IMF lifted Japan’s 2017 growth projection by 0.4 percentage point from January, to 1.2 per cent, while the euro zone and China both saw a 0.1 percentage point growth forecast increase to 1.7 per cent and 6.6 per cent, respectively.
Additional reporting: Reuters

This adjustment is attributed to favorable financial market conditions and a cyclical rebound in manufacturing and trade. The Washington-based institution now anticipates global growth to reach 3.5 percent in 2017, an increase from the 3.4 percent forecast issued in January and a rise from the 3.1 percent growth recorded in the previous year. The IMF’s projection for 2018 remains unchanged at 3.6 percent.

Despite these positive developments, the report cautions that persistent structural constraints continue to inhibit a more robust recovery. It notes that the balance of risks remains skewed to the downside, particularly over the medium term. The IMF identifies enduring challenges, including subdued productivity growth and elevated income inequality. Furthermore, it warns that inward-looking policy orientations pose a threat to global economic integration and the cooperative international economic order, which have historically benefited the global economy, especially emerging market and developing economies.

Regarding specific economies, the IMF has revised the United Kingdom’s 2017 growth forecast upward by half a percentage point to 2.0 percent, noting that the negative economic consequences of the Brexit referendum have been slower to manifest than initially anticipated. The growth forecast for the United States in 2017 is maintained at 2.3 percent, a significant acceleration from the 1.6 percent growth observed in 2016, partly reflecting expectations of fiscal stimulus. Japan’s 2017 growth outlook was raised by 0.4 percentage points to 1.2 percent. Modest upward revisions of 0.1 percentage points were also applied to the euro area and China, bringing their respective growth forecasts to 1.7 percent and 6.6 percent for the year.

DETROIT (AP) - Detroit Tigers pitching prospect Franklin Perez is expected to miss at least three months with a right lat strain.
The Tigers say Perez was injured in a minor league game Sunday. There is no surgery recommended at this point, but the recovery is expected to take a minimum of 12 weeks.
Perez, a 20-year-old right-hander, was acquired by Detroit in the trade that sent Justin Verlander to Houston last season. Perez went 6-3 with a 3.02 ERA across two levels of the minors last year. Sending children off to college or into the real world is usually a proud time for parents. But there also can be sadness, especially when it's the last child to leave home. Empty nest syndrome isn't a clinical diagnosis. Instead, it's a phenomenon in which parents experience feelings of sadness and loss when the last child leaves home.
"It's common for parents to find letting go to be a painful experience — even though they actively encourage their children to be independent," says Dr. Jessica Sosso, Family Medicine, Mayo Clinic Health System. "Parents might find it difficult to suddenly have no children at home who need their care. They might miss being a part of their children's daily lives and their constant companionship. Parents with only one child or those who strongly identify with their role as a parent might have a particularly difficult time adjusting."
Sosso explains that as hard as the change may be, having an empty nest can bring benefits to parents. Recent studies suggest that an empty nest might reduce work and family conflicts. Having an empty nest also gives parents a new opportunity to reconnect with each other, improve the quality of their marriage and rekindle interests for which they previously might not have had time.
If you're experiencing feelings of loss due to empty nest syndrome, Sosso suggests these tips:

Screams erupted from the audience as Davro, who could not break the fall as a result of being in the stocks, fell face first.

Chegwin accused Roman Polanski of asking him to remove his underwear (Joel Ryan/PA)

“There was one scene where we all run into a banqueting hall and go to sleep for the night, and he just looked at Martin Shaw and me and said: ‘Take your underpants off.’
“And he was the boss so you go: ‘Fine, OK.’ We just did it. Couldn’t work out why; still don’t know why.”

rewrite:
Keith Chegwin’s professional trajectory encompassed a diverse range of roles, from presenting the popular children’s programme *Multi-Coloured Swap Shop* to a later appearance on *Celebrity Big Brother*. The presenter, further recognised for hosting the children’s game show *Cheggers Plays Pop*, passed away at the age of 60 following a struggle with a progressive pulmonary illness. The following outlines several notable incidents from his career and life.

Firstly, during a television recording, Chegwin was observed reacting with visible alarm as comedian Bobby Davro fell forward, striking the floor with his face. Davro, who was restrained in stocks at the time, was unable to arrest his fall, prompting audible distress from the studio audience. The incident resulted in Davro sustaining torn ligaments in his back and requiring sutures to his chin. Subsequently, Davro publicly reflected on their friendship via social media, stating: “I have known Keith Chegwin for many years. He was one of the nicest guys I've ever met in this business. I had been told he was very poorly but unable to contact him for a while. What a dreadful shame to lose such a lovely friend. Love to his family. RIP Cheggers! I'll miss that smile 💔” (Davro, 2017).

Secondly, in a 1992 appearance on the programme *This Morning*, Chegwin disclosed his personal struggle with alcohol dependency. He addressed presenters Richard Madeley and Judy Finnigan with candour, stating, “I am an alcoholic. It’s a disease.”

Thirdly, Chegwin recounted an unsettling experience from his adolescence while working on Roman Polanski’s 1971 film adaptation of *Macbeth*. In a 2011 interview with *The Telegraph*, he alleged that the director instructed him and fellow actor Martin Shaw to remove their underwear during a particular scene, an instruction they felt compelled to obey without understanding the rationale, citing Polanski’s authoritative position.

Finally, in an illustrative example of his unconventional broadcasting style, Chegwin once conducted an impromptu interview for Channel 4’s *The Big Breakfast* by approaching Steve Coogan at his hotel room the morning after a BAFTA ceremony. Coogan’s acquiescence led to the camera crew inadvertently capturing the presence of his girlfriend in the room, a moment broadcast to viewers.

(Source: Press Association, 2017)

Police investigate armed robbery on Lionel Street
By News-Argus Staff
Published in News on October 6, 2017 10:19 AM
Goldsboro police are investigating after a man was robbed at gunpoint on Lionel Street Thursday afternoon, according to a police incident report.
According to the report, a man was walking on the 100 block of Lionel Street just after noon Thursday, when he heard a vehicle approach him from behind. When the vehicle drove up next to him, the driver rolled the window down, pointed a handgun at him and yelled "Give it up, man."
The victim responded "I don't have anything to give you," prompting the suspect to exit the vehicle and walk toward the victim. The suspect then took the victim's smartphone, valued at $100, and left moving north on Lionel Street, according to the report.
Police Major Anthony Carmon said that the police department has a suspect in the case, but that suspect has not been charged with anything yet.

The driver subsequently lowered the window, brandished a handgun, and demanded the victim surrender his belongings. Following the victim’s verbal refusal, the suspect exited the vehicle, confronted the victim directly, and seized the victim’s smartphone, which is valued at approximately one hundred dollars. The suspect then departed the scene, traveling northbound on Lionel Street. Police Major Anthony Carmon indicated that while a person of interest has been identified in connection with the case, no formal charges have been filed at this time. England may have qualified for the World Cup following Thursday's scruffy 1-0 win over Slovenia but manager Gareth Southgate admits they have a "hell of a lot of work to do" if they are to be contenders in Russia next year.
Captain Harry Kane grabbed an injury-time winner at Wembley to secure top spot in Group F but it was another unconvincing display from Southgate's players and the former Middlesbrough boss knows they must improve over the next eight months.
"I think this team has potential, but we've got a hell of a lot of work to do," he told ITV Sport.
"They've come here on the back of what happened in the last European Championships, they've had the change of coach, they've had a lot of difficulties to deal with through the campaign.
"But we're there [at the World Cup] and now we build and we look to where we can improve all the time.
"Joe Hart [made] big saves at important times and that's where his experience has come through.
"We know where we have to do better but that's for tomorrow. Tonight, we go to the World Cup and that's fantastic."
Late goals have underpinned England's successful qualifying campaign - Kane scored a late equaliser away to Scotland in June, while Adam Lallana struck deep in stoppage-time to earn a 1-0 win in Slovakia in September 2016, which turned out to be Sam Allardyce's sole game in charge.
And Southgate believes it is no coincidence it happened again on Thursday.
Job done! Qualified for the World Cup! A really great feeling. 👌 #ThreeLions 🦁🦁🦁 pic.twitter.com/ELzNGYoq5B — Harry Kane (@HKane) October 5, 2017
"We played a team who have only conceded four goals in the competition - and you saw why," Southgate added.
"They defended resolutely, they broke the game up when they had to, they took yellow cards when they had to.
"We weren't quite as sharp as we hoped to be with the ball. But we stuck at it and it's not a coincidence if you keep scoring late goals.
"Late goals have been key and we knew they had to win. We changed formation to go two up front at the end."
rewrite:
England secured qualification for the World Cup following a narrow 1-0 victory over Slovenia on Thursday, yet manager Gareth Southgate acknowledged a substantial amount of progress is required if the team is to be considered a genuine contender at next year’s tournament in Russia. The winning goal, scored by captain Harry Kane during injury time at Wembley Stadium, ensured first place in Group F. However, the performance was once again unconvincing, leading Southgate—the former Middlesbrough manager—to emphasize the necessity for improvement over the coming eight months.

In a post-match interview with ITV Sport, Southgate stated, “This team possesses potential, but we have a considerable amount of work ahead. The players have operated under the shadow of the previous European Championships, experienced a change in coaching leadership, and confronted numerous challenges throughout this qualifying campaign. Nevertheless, we have achieved qualification, and we now must build upon this foundation while continuously seeking areas for enhancement.” He highlighted the contribution of goalkeeper Joe Hart, whose critical saves demonstrated valuable experience. Southgate concluded, “We are aware of the aspects requiring improvement, but that assessment can wait. For now, securing World Cup participation is a commendable achievement.”

Late goals have been a defining characteristic of England’s successful qualification effort. Kane previously scored a late equalizer against Scotland in June, while Adam Lallana secured a stoppage-time winner against Slovakia in September 2016—a result that marked Sam Allardyce’s only match in charge. Southgate suggested it was not coincidental that a similar pattern emerged against Slovenia. “We faced an opponent that had conceded only four goals throughout the competition, and their defensive resilience was evident,” he observed. “They defended resolutely, disrupted play effectively, and accepted tactical cautions when necessary. Our offensive sharpness was below our expectations, yet we persisted. Scoring late goals repeatedly is not a matter of chance; it has been a crucial element of our campaign. Recognizing Slovenia’s need to win, we adjusted our formation to employ two forwards in the latter stages, which ultimately contributed to the outcome.”

How long does it take to make a life-altering decision? Netflix’s new series Seven Seconds asks viewers just that as it takes the audience down a dark and all-too-real rabbit hole.
Seven Seconds, created by Veena Sud, follows the aftermath and investigation into a hit-and-run that killed Brenton Butler, a black teenager in Jersey City. Viewers watch as the cops who were involved in the accident try to cover their tracks and the Butler family reels from the crime. The show also allows the audience to look into the lives of the lawyer, KJ Harper, prosecuting the case and Fish, the detective who pushes Harper to look deeper into the case.
This drama is a must-see series, even though it can be hard to watch as the unfolding events feel as though they have been ripped directly from the headlines. What makes this story so compelling is how it portrays the aftermath of the accident.
The acting in this series is phenomenal. Regina King and Russell Hornsby’s heartwrenching performances as Brenton Butler’s parents make the drama all the more tragic. Yes, the couple loses their son, but as the investigation drags on and the hope of getting justice for their son drifts farther away, they find themselves pushing the other away in their grief. It is through their love of their son that the audience learns who Brenton Butler was.
Beau Knapp, as Peter Jablonski, the driver of this tragedy, portrays a man racked with guilt over his actions and fear of what will happen to him if he comes forward. Clare-Hope Ashitey performs beautifully as the self-pitying and disillusioned and often intoxicated KJ Harper.
Seven Seconds is available on Netflix and has 10 hour-long episodes. The series is rated TV-MA. Fans of Seven Seconds may also enjoy The Killing, another series by Veena Sud, which follows the lives of two detectives as they investigate murders. Those looking for lighter fare should give Netflix’s Nailed It a try. It’s an amusing baking competition where amatuer bakers try to recreate fancy cakes to win the prize.
rewrite:
The Netflix series *Seven Seconds*, created by Veena Sud, examines the protracted and complex nature of life-altering decisions through a grimly realistic narrative. The program meticulously traces the investigation following a hit-and-run accident that results in the death of Brenton Butler, an African American adolescent in Jersey City. The narrative unfolds across two primary trajectories: the concerted efforts by the implicated police officers to conceal their involvement, and the profound devastation experienced by the Butler family. Further perspective is provided through the characters of KJ Harper, the attorney prosecuting the case, and Detective "Fish," whose insistence compels a more thorough inquiry.

While the series presents a challenging viewing experience due to its resonance with contemporary socio-political headlines, this very quality underscores its significance. The drama's compelling power lies in its nuanced exploration of the accident's aftermath, extending beyond the immediate event to depict the corrosive effects on all involved. The performances are critically noteworthy, particularly the portrayals by Regina King and Russell Hornsby as the bereaved parents. Their heartrending performances illustrate not only the tragedy of loss but also the subsequent marital estrangement that emerges as the pursuit of justice becomes increasingly futile. Their shared grief serves as the primary vehicle for revealing the identity of the deceased.

Beau Knapp delivers a compelling performance as Peter Jablonski, the driver, embodying a character tormented by guilt and fear. Clare-Hope Ashitey similarly excels in her depiction of KJ Harper, capturing the attorney's disillusionment and personal struggles with palpable authenticity. Comprising ten hour-long episodes rated TV-MA, *Seven Seconds* is available for streaming on Netflix. Viewers who appreciate its procedural and thematic depth may also find value in *The Killing*, another series by Veena Sud. For those seeking contrasting content, the amateur baking competition *Nailed It* offers a notably more lighthearted alternative.

Meet Ryan. He’s 6 years old, likes to play with toys, and has just been listed as one of Forbes’ highest-earning YouTube celebrities. Per Business Insider, the young entrepreneur, who hosts his family’s Ryan ToysReview channel on the video-sharing site, helped his household bring in about $11 million in pretax income this year, simply by opening toys and other products and reviewing them online.
This monetized mastery of the “unboxing” phenomenon—what the Verge has described as “a blend of innocent childhood antics and relentless, often overwhelming consumerism”—places Ryan’s channel in the No. 8 slot on the Forbes list (tied with the slapstick team Smosh), alongside other big YouTube names like brothers Jake and Logan Paul, Minecraft whiz Daniel “DanTDM” Middleton, and the controversial PewDiePie (real name: Felix Kjellberg).
What makes Ryan unusual is, obviously, his age. “He is definitely the youngest YouTube star we’ve ever seen,” an industry analyst told the Verge in last December’s profile.
Ryan’s parents posted his first video in March 2015 after the YouTube-obsessed preschooler wanted to know why he couldn’t dish on toys online like other kids, per a Tubefilter interview from last year.
In July of that year, the family experienced its first viral video: Ryan opening a “giant egg surprise” with more than 100 Cars-branded toys. The channel has exploded since, now with over 10 million subscribers and more than 16 million views, per the Washington Post.
Ryan’s parents told Tubefilter they mainly film on the weekends so it doesn’t interfere with their son’s schooling and that they pay for all of the toys Ryan reviews.

President Donald Trump celebrated active-duty service members and veterans during a military tribute on the eve of Independence Day.

ELKHART, Ind. -- It’s something no one wants to come across: a 6-inch spider.
An employee at Godfrey Marine encountered it while building a boat at work. Jacob Collins, who shared photos of the spider on Facebook, didn’t know what to think at first.
He later found out it was a fishing spider—something the Indiana Department of Natural Resources said is relatively harmless despite its terrifying look. The spider’s three-inch leg span allows it to walk on water. It's often mistaken for a wolf spider, one of the most common large spiders found in Indiana.
Collins and his co-workers caught the fishing spider and snapped a few photos of the impressive specimen. They then released it back into the wild.
"They found this giant beast on a boat at work today," Collins wrote in his post. "Beware all Elkhart [County] residents. They are out there and they are real."
As of Thursday morning, his Facebook post about the spider had more than 8,100 shares and hundreds of comments.
rewrite:
A recent incident at Godfrey Marine in Elkhart, Indiana, involved the discovery of a sizable arachnid with a leg span of approximately six inches. An employee, Jacob Collins, encountered the specimen during boat assembly and subsequently documented the find on social media. Initial uncertainty regarding its identification was resolved upon consultation with the Indiana Department of Natural Resources, which confirmed the specimen as a fishing spider (*Dolomedes* spp.). Although its appearance is formidable, the species is considered relatively harmless to humans. Notably, its morphological adaptations, including a three-inch leg span, facilitate locomotion on aquatic surfaces. It is frequently misidentified as a wolf spider, a more common large spider indigenous to the region.

Following its capture and photographic documentation, the spider was released unharmed. Collins’s accompanying social media post, which cautioned local residents, garnered significant engagement, accruing over 8,100 shares and hundreds of comments by Thursday morning.

Court papers released Tuesday say 25-year-old Enrique Marquez Jr. agreed to plead guilty to conspiring to provide material support to terrorists and lying when he purchased two rifles used in the 2015 attack.
Mandy Pifer's boyfriend, Shannon Johnson, was among 14 people killed in the attack at the Inland Regional Center.

3 p.m.
Court records say a man accused of buying high-powered rifles used in the San Bernardino terror attack has agreed to plead guilty to federal criminal charges.
The documents released Tuesday say Enrique Marquez Jr. has agreed to plead guilty to conspiring to provide material support to terrorists and one other charge.
Prosecutors say Marquez acknowledged plotting with Syed Rizwan Farook in 2011 and 2012 to massacre college students and gun down motorists on a gridlocked freeway. Those attacks never occurred.
Authorities said Marquez purchased the guns used by Farook and his wife, Tashfeen Malik, in the Dec. 2, 2015, attack in which 14 people were killed at a public health agency event before the suspects died in a gunfight with police.
rewrite:
Enrique Marquez Jr., a defendant charged in connection with the 2015 San Bernardino terrorist attack, has entered into a plea agreement with federal prosecutors. According to court documents unsealed on Tuesday, the 25-year-old has agreed to plead guilty to charges of conspiring to provide material support to terrorists and making false statements during the purchase of firearms. These firearms, two high-powered rifles, were subsequently used in the December 2, 2015, assault on the Inland Regional Center, which resulted in the deaths of fourteen individuals.

The plea agreement reveals that Marquez had previously engaged in terrorist plotting with Syed Rizwan Farook, one of the two perpetrators of the San Bernardino attack, during 2011 and 2012. Their abandoned plans allegedly included a mass shooting targeting college students and an attack on motorists during freeway gridlock. Prosecutors state that Marquez later purchased the weapons utilized by Farook and his wife, Tashfeen Malik, in the executed attack at a public health agency event. The assailants were subsequently killed in an exchange of gunfire with law enforcement.

The development has elicited a complex response from victims’ families. Mandy Pifer, whose boyfriend Shannon Johnson was killed in the attack, described experiencing mixed emotions. While expressing relief that the legal proceedings against Marquez will avoid a protracted trial, she emphasized that the outcome cannot restore her loss. Pifer intends to deliver a victim impact statement at Marquez’s forthcoming sentencing hearing.

Hundreds of hardy Brummie clubbers shrugged off the Beast from the East 2.0 this weekend - braving the cold in minuscule dresses and thin shorts.
Revellers gathered at Birmingham's popular nightspot to celebrate St Patrick's Day despite the Met Office warning partygoers not to venture out in the 'dangerously cold' winds and snow.
Police advised Brummies to wrap up warm with several layers, but that didn't thwart clubbers' plans to don next-to-nothing outfits on Broad Street this Saturday.
Women were pictured strutting from bar to bar across the ice-covered strip in six-inch heels and sleeveless dresses as the 'mini Beast from the East' blasted the city cente.
Some favoured the ripped-jean look in a bid to stay warm in the freezing temperatures, but could still be seen shivering outside Broad Street's popular haunts.
Revellers were also photographed huddling under the shelter of phonebooths and bar entrances in hope of escaping the weather.
And it wasn't just the women either, men stepped out into the snow in short sleeve shirts and shorts as part of their traditional Irish fancy dress.
Fortunately for the fearless clubbers, warmer forecasts are on the horizon with temperatures of 8C set towards the end of the week.
This is the forecast for this week so far.
Today's forecast:
After a very cold start, it should be a dry and fine day with sunny spells. Remaining breezy but with lighter winds than on Sunday. Temperatures recovering closer to average. Maximum temperature 6 °C.
Outlook for Tuesday to Thursday:
After a frosty start, dry and fine on Tuesday with lighter winds. Turning more unsettled thereafter with spells of rain and strengthening winds, although with temperatures recovering closer to average.
Temperatures will reach a relatively balmy 8C on Thursday.
rewrite:
Despite severe meteorological warnings, a significant number of individuals in Birmingham participated in St Patrick's Day celebrations this past weekend, disregarding the hazardous conditions brought by a cold weather system colloquially termed "the Beast from the East 2.0." The Met Office had explicitly advised against unnecessary travel due to perilously low temperatures, strong winds, and snowfall. Official guidance from local police recommended wearing multiple layers for warmth. Nevertheless, attendees at various establishments along Broad Street opted for attire ill-suited to the climate, including sleeveless dresses, shorts, and high-heeled footwear, frequently navigating icy pavements.

Observations indicated that many participants experienced visible discomfort from the cold, with numerous individuals seeking temporary refuge in sheltered areas such as doorways and under awnings. This behavior was not gender-specific; both men and women were noted wearing summer-style clothing, with some men adopting shorts and short-sleeved shirts as part of festive attire. A minority attempted to incorporate more substantial garments, such as ripped jeans, though these too proved largely inadequate against the freezing conditions.

In contrast to the weekend's extreme weather, meteorological projections indicate a forthcoming moderation in temperatures. The immediate forecast suggests a dry day with intermittent sunshine and lighter winds, culminating in a maximum temperature of approximately 6°C. The outlook for the subsequent period, Tuesday through Thursday, predicts initially frosty conditions giving way to more unsettled weather patterns, including periods of rain and strengthening winds. Notably, temperatures are expected to rise, approaching seasonal averages, with a peak of around 8°C anticipated by Thursday. This anticipated warming will likely provide relief from the recent severe cold snap.

More than half the cells in your body are not human according to researchers.
More than half the cells in your body are not human according to researchers. iStock
NEARLY 60 per cent of cells in the body are not actually human, according to scientists.
Human cells make up just 43 per cent of our total cell count, while the rest are microscopic tenants that are essential for our wellbeing.
The hidden half of our body is called our microbiome, and experts studying it could unlock new ways of tackling diseases, from allergy to Parkinson's.
Microscopic creatures, including bacteria, viruses, fungi and archaea, cover your entire body.
"They are essential to your health,” says Prof Ruth Ley, of the Max Planck Institute, "your body isn't just you”.
The highest concentration of this microscopic life lives in our oxygen-deprived bowels.
Prof Rob Knight, from University of California San Diego, told the BBC: "You're more microbe than you are human.”
At first, boffs thought our cells were outnumbered 10 to one, but the prof said: "That's been refined much closer to one-to-one, so the current estimate is you're about 43% human if you're counting up all the cells”.
Scientists are rapidly uncovering the role microbial material plays in digestion, regulating the immune system, protecting against disease and manufacturing vital vitamins.
Prof Knight said: "We're finding ways that these tiny creatures totally transform our health in ways we never imagined until recently.”
This article originally appeared on The Sun and has been republished with permission.
rewrite:
Contemporary scientific research indicates that a substantial proportion of the cells constituting the human body are not of human origin. Estimates suggest that approximately 43 percent of the total cellular count consists of human cells, with the remaining majority comprising a diverse assemblage of microorganisms, collectively termed the microbiome. This microbial community, which includes bacteria, viruses, fungi, and archaea, colonizes various bodily surfaces and is now understood to be fundamental to physiological homeostasis.

The microbiome is particularly concentrated within the gastrointestinal tract, an environment characterized by low oxygen availability. As Professor Ruth Ley of the Max Planck Institute notes, these microbial inhabitants are essential to health, fundamentally challenging the conception of the body as a purely human entity. This perspective is echoed by Professor Rob Knight of the University of California San Diego, who observes that an individual is quantitatively more microbial than human. Early approximations suggesting a ten-to-one ratio of microbial to human cells have been refined; current consensus, as cited by Professor Knight, approximates a near one-to-one ratio, with human cells constituting roughly 43 percent of the total.

Ongoing investigation is rapidly elucidating the critical functions of this microbial material, which encompass aiding digestion, modulating immune system activity, providing protection against pathogens, and synthesizing essential vitamins. Consequently, as Professor Knight emphasizes, research is revealing that these microorganisms profoundly influence health in previously unanticipated ways. The study of the microbiome thus represents a promising frontier for developing novel therapeutic interventions for a range of conditions, from allergic disorders to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's.

By Scott T. Sterling
With the band’s third album, What If Nothing, on the horizon, Ohio rock band Walk the Moon has opened up about the process behind its creation.
Related: Walk The Moon Debut ‘One Foot’ Video
“The approach was just making noise, getting back to our roots of being a rock & roll band and just playing our instruments and letting the sound bounce off the walls,” singer Nicholas Petricca explained to Rolling Stone
“Sonically, we’re reaching for taller, wider, and more vast, more epic sounds,” he said. “But the lyrics are kind of the opposite. They’re much more personal and are very close to the heart, very raw.”
Despite the “chaos” that went into the new full-length, including the band canceling a tour last summer when Petricca’s father fell ill, the singer is pleased with how What If Nothing ultimately turned out.
“There’s this feeling where everything is like a bad haircut, and everything feels unfinished,” he revealed. “That moment of getting the record beyond the point of discomfort, until the record is to the point of, ‘Oh. What a relief. This feels amazing,’ is a major lesson in trust – you really are just faced with having to trust yourself and your collaborators and the producer that this deformed laboratory monster is going to, eventually, grow wings and become something really beautiful.”
rewrite:
In anticipation of the forthcoming third album *What If Nothing*, the Ohio-based rock ensemble Walk the Moon has detailed the creative methodology underlying its production. Frontman Nicholas Petricca, in a discussion with *Rolling Stone*, characterized the approach as a return to foundational principles: “The methodology centered on generating noise, reconnecting with our origins as a rock & roll band by simply playing our instruments and allowing sound to resonate organically.” He further elaborated on the album’s dichotomous nature, noting, “Sonically, we are aspiring toward more expansive, grander, and epic textures. Conversely, the lyrical content is markedly more intimate, heartfelt, and emotionally exposed.”

This new full-length project emerged amidst considerable turmoil, including the cancellation of a tour following the illness of Petricca’s father. Nevertheless, the vocalist expresses satisfaction with the final outcome. He describes the creative process as navigating a phase where “everything resembles a poor haircut and feels incomplete.” Petricca emphasizes that progressing the record beyond this point of acute discomfort to a stage of profound relief constitutes a critical exercise in trust. This necessitates faith in oneself, one’s collaborators, and the producer, with the belief that the initial, seemingly “deformed laboratory monster” of a project will ultimately develop its wings and transform into something of genuine beauty.

“American Animals” takes an appropriately wild approach to its subject, biting off a little more than it can chew, but nevertheless coming up with a truly novel entry in the overcrowded heist genre.
In his feature debut, director/writer Bart Layton chronicles the odd but true story of four young men who hatched an elaborate scheme to steal rare books from a Kentucky university in 2004, the grand prize being John James Audubon’s enormous tome “Birds of America.”
Layton mixes truth and fiction with abandon, enlisting the real four men to chime in alongside the actors playing their younger selves. As ringleader Warren, the charismatic Evan Peters (“X-Men Apocalypse”) convinces his stoner artist buddy Spencer (Barry Keoghan) that a grand, no-one-gets-hurt robbery is just what they need to shake off the yoke of life’s encroaching normalcy.
Early on, the film’s tone is light, with the real Warren and Spencer questioning each other’s renditions of how it all went down. As they enlist more humorless pals Eric (Jared Abrahamson) and Chas (Blake Jenner), though, the proceedings get increasingly dark.
By the time Warren’s squaring his shoulders to tase the rare-books librarian (Ann Dowd, always a treat), “American Animals” has veered from sorta-true-crime quasi-comedy into a Scorsese-inflected look at the realities of attempting a theft of this magnitude.
Sweat, tears, vomit and rage replace the usual smooth stylings of a cinematic heist, and although this might not all tonally flow, it’s clear you’re watching a dazzling new directorial career taking flight.
rewrite:
Bart Layton’s feature debut, *American Animals*, offers a formally inventive contribution to the well-populated heist genre, adopting an ambitious—if occasionally overextended—approach to its source material. The film documents the peculiar but factual 2004 conspiracy by four young men to steal valuable rare books, most notably John James Audubon’s *Birds of America*, from a Kentucky university library. Layton deliberately blurs the boundaries between documentary and dramatization, intercutting interviews with the actual perpetrators alongside scenes featuring actors who portray their younger selves. This narrative strategy introduces a reflexive commentary on memory and truth from the outset, as the real Warren Lipka and Spencer Reinhard dispute each other’s accounts of events.

The initial tone is comparatively light, charting how Warren (played with charismatic volatility by Evan Peters) persuades the more reticent Spencer (Barry Keoghan) that an ambitious, non-violent theft could liberate them from mundane suburban futures. However, as the group expands to include the more severe figures of Eric Borsuk (Jared Abrahamson) and Chas Allen (Blake Jenner), the film’s mood darkens considerably. The climax of the heist itself, involving the tasering of a librarian (Ann Dowd), marks a decisive tonal shift. The film transitions from a quasi-comedic true-crime narrative into a gritty, almost Scorsese-esque examination of the visceral realities of criminal undertaking. Conventional heist-movie slickness is replaced by sweat, panic, and physical disgust. While the resulting tonal modulation is not entirely seamless, the film ultimately succeeds as a compelling and audacious directorial statement, signaling the arrival of a distinctive cinematic voice.

1. Take a day off from the news, one day a week.
2. Don’t get into an argument with a Trump supporter, especially if it’s a member of your family. Remember, there are more independents and non-voters than Trump Republicans. And the 2018 midterm election will be won on the basis of turnout.
3. Pay no attention to Trump’s tweets. They’re becoming increasingly bizarre and irrelevant.
4. Watch an old movie of biting political satire, like Wag the Dog.
5. But don’t watch Doctor Strangelove.
6. Join an Indivisible group near you and take action with them, attending a congressional town meeting and organizing others to contact your members of congress. It’s having an effect. Plus, it’s therapeutic.
7. Drink lots of water and get plenty of exercise. It helps with the anger.
8. Read good books of fiction, like the Harry Potter series. Don’t read George Orwell’s 1984 or Sinclair Lewis’s It Can’t Happen Here, or Philip Roth’s The Plot Against America.
9. Go to a county fair with your kids, and watch the pigs.
10. Have a cookout with your neighbors and see what resources you can offer to your community. Start a tool collective or teach a class in a library or out of someone’s house. Tangible change can come from your hands, not only your votes. Remember, resistance works best when people come together and work together.
Have a great summer!
This article was originally published at RobertReich.org. It has been edited for YES! Magazine.
rewrite:
To maintain psychological well-being and civic efficacy amidst contemporary political tensions, consider adopting the following practices. First, designate one day per week to abstain from consuming news media. Second, refrain from engaging in contentious debates with supporters of former President Trump, particularly within familial settings. Electoral outcomes, such as the 2018 midterms, are often determined by voter turnout, which involves mobilizing a broader coalition of independents and non-voters rather than persuading entrenched partisans. Third, disregard the content of Trump’s social media posts, as they frequently diverge from substantive political discourse.

Fourth, view classic films offering sharp political satire, such as *Wag the Dog*, while avoiding dystopian narratives like *Doctor Strangelove*. Fifth, participate in local activist organizations, like Indivisible groups, by attending town hall meetings and coordinating constituent outreach to congressional representatives. Such engagement proves both politically impactful and psychologically beneficial. Sixth, prioritize physical health through adequate hydration and regular exercise to mitigate stress.

Seventh, select fiction for leisure reading, opting for works like the Harry Potter series over politically ominous novels such as *1984*, *It Can’t Happen Here*, or *The Plot Against America*. Eighth, partake in community activities, such as visiting a county fair with family. Ninth, organize neighborhood gatherings to identify shared resources and skills, such as establishing a tool library or offering community classes. Tangible local action, complementing electoral participation, fosters resilience and demonstrates that collective grassroots efforts remain a potent form of civic resistance.

A drug-driver who was involved in a crash on the M1 was unable to stand up when highways officers arrived.
Police then found he could not drive in a straight line.
Cameron Gutherie, 19, of Sutton Road, Church Broughton, was involved in the collision with another vehicle on the southbound carriageway of the M1 motorway, near Tibshelf services.
Highways officers attended the scene and advised the drivers off both cars, who were uninjured, to travel to the services to get them off the motorway and exchange details.
But Lynn Bickley, prosecuting, said: "Mr Gutherie appeared to be unable to drive in a straight line and highways officers noticed the Vauxhall Corsa he was driving mount a kerb and stall. There was a wheel-spin and then the car sped off in the direction of the car park.
(Image: Google Maps)
“He appeared unable to stand up and was advised to remain seated in his car while the police were called. The defendant appeared to fall asleep and remained like that until police arrived at 7.50am.”
Mrs Bickley added that police had to wake Gutherie and they felt that he appeared intoxicated or under the influence of drugs.
The teenager completed a road-side drink-drive test which was negative but traces of a drug were found in his system after a blood test.
Mrs Bickley confirmed that the drug Alprazolam - which is used to treat anxiety - was found in Gutherie’s system. This can have side effects including drowsiness and nausea.
The business management student pleaded guilty to driving a vehicle while unfit to drive through drugs after the incident on October 22 at Chesterfield magistrates’ court.
Defence solicitor Paul McLeod said the defendant has a history of depression and he had been to a party. He was feeling down and his friends had advised him to leave and had given him a tablet to make him feel better.
Magistrates fined Gutherie £120 and ordered him to pay £85 costs and a £30 victim surcharge.
He was also banned from driving for 12 months.
rewrite:
A motorist involved in a collision on the M1 motorway was found to be incapable of standing upon the arrival of highways officers. Subsequent observations by police indicated he was also unable to operate his vehicle in a linear trajectory. The individual, Cameron Gutherie, a 19-year-old from Sutton Road, Church Broughton, was implicated in a crash with another vehicle on the southbound carriageway near Tibshelf services. Following the incident, highways personnel attended the scene and directed the drivers, both of whom were unharmed, to proceed to the services area to facilitate their removal from the motorway and the exchange of particulars.

As detailed by prosecutor Lynn Bickley, Mr. Gutherie exhibited an apparent inability to drive in a straight line. Highways officers observed the Vauxhall Corsa he was operating mount a kerb and stall, followed by a wheel-spin before the vehicle accelerated toward the car park. Furthermore, Mr. Gutherie appeared unable to stand and was advised to remain seated within his vehicle while law enforcement was summoned. The defendant subsequently appeared to fall asleep and remained in that state until police arrived at 7:50 a.m.

Mrs. Bickley added that officers were required to awaken Mr. Gutherie and formed the opinion that he seemed intoxicated or under the influence of substances. A preliminary roadside breath test for alcohol yielded a negative result; however, a subsequent blood analysis confirmed the presence of a drug in his system. The prosecution specified the substance as Alprazolam, a medication prescribed for anxiety, known to have side effects encompassing drowsiness and nausea.

The defendant, a business management student, entered a guilty plea at Chesterfield Magistrates’ Court to the charge of driving a vehicle while unfit due to drugs, relating to the event on October 22. Defence solicitor Paul McLeod submitted that his client has a documented history of depression. On the occasion in question, Mr. Gutherie had attended a party, was experiencing low mood, and was advised by friends to depart. They provided him with a tablet intended to improve his disposition. The magistrates imposed a fine of £120, with additional orders to pay £85 in costs and a £30 victim surcharge. A twelve-month driving disqualification was also levied.

Hamilton has now officially become an at-risk area for Lyme disease after the city’s public health officials found blacklegged ticks at the Christie Lake Conservation Area in consecutive seasons.
Susan Harding-Cruz, Hamilton’s manager of vector-borne diseases, told the city’s Board of Health March 19 after “tick dragging” studies were conducted last spring and fall they revealed a total of 13 ticks were identified at the conservation area, along with at Borer’s Falls and the Royal Botanical Gardens. She said only at Christie Lake Conservation Area did the city find ticks in the fall and spring seasons. Those ticks all tested negative for Lyme disease.
But, she said, another eight blacklegged ticks, also referred to as deer ticks of 78 that were received by the public tested positive for Lyme disease. She said five of the ticks were from Dundas and two were located in Binbrook.
Blacklegged ticks are usually found in woodlands, tall grasses and bushes.
It means, said Harding-Cruz, a 20-kilometre radius from Christie Lake Conservation Area, which takes in most of Hamilton except Stoney Creek and Binbrook, becomes an “estimated risk area” for ticks.
Hamilton will be included on a map of estimated risk areas for Lyme disease this year that is distributed by Public Health Ontario. Other at-risk areas from last year include the Niagara Region, Turkey Point, Pickering and most of eastern Ontario.
Hamilton residents should take precautions when venturing into long grass such as using DEET, wear long-sleeves and pants, and shoes with closed toes.
Harding-Cruz said if a person finds a tick on them, they should remove it. Harding-Cruz said ticks have six legs in the larval stage and eight legs when they are adults.
Lyme disease is infectious that is caused by bacteria spread by ticks. The most common sign of infection is an expanding area of redness on the skin that starts at the point of the tick bite.
Symptoms could include fever, headache and feeling tired. If left untreated a person could experience the paralysis of the face, joint pains, and severe headaches with neck stiffness or heart palpitations. The tick usually must be attached to a person for up to 48 hours before the bacteria can spread.
rewrite:
Hamilton has been formally designated an area of risk for Lyme disease following the identification of blacklegged ticks (*Ixodes scapularis*) within the Christie Lake Conservation Area over successive surveillance seasons. This declaration was issued by Hamilton Public Health Services after systematic "tick dragging" surveys conducted in the spring and autumn of the preceding year. Presenting to the Hamilton Board of Health on March 19, Susan Harding-Cruz, Manager of Vector-Borne Diseases, reported that these surveys resulted in the collection of 13 blacklegged ticks from Christie Lake Conservation Area, with additional specimens located at Borer’s Falls and the Royal Botanical Gardens. Notably, Christie Lake was the sole location where ticks were recovered during both seasonal surveys. Laboratory analysis confirmed that all ticks collected via active surveillance tested negative for the bacterium *Borrelia burgdorferi*, which causes Lyme disease.

However, Harding-Cruz further reported that of 78 ticks submitted by the public for identification and testing, eight blacklegged ticks were positive for Lyme disease. Geographic data indicated that five of these positive ticks originated from Dundas, with two from Binbrook. As blacklegged ticks are typically endemic to wooded habitats, tall grasses, and brush, this passive surveillance data is critical for risk assessment. Based on established public health parameters, the discovery of ticks through active surveillance at Christie Lake triggers the classification of an estimated risk area. Consequently, a 20-kilometre radius from that location—encompassing most of Hamilton with the exception of Stoney Creek and Binbrook—is now designated as such. Hamilton will accordingly be included on the annual map of estimated risk areas for Lyme disease distributed by Public Health Ontario, joining other previously identified regions including the Niagara Region, Turkey Point, Pickering, and much of eastern Ontario.

Residents are advised to adopt protective measures when in areas of potential tick habitat, such as wearing long sleeves, long pants, and closed-toe footwear, and using insect repellent containing DEET. Should an attached tick be discovered, prompt and careful removal is recommended. Harding-Cruz noted that identifying features include six legs in the larval stage and eight legs in the nymph and adult stages. Lyme disease is a bacterial infection transmitted through tick bites. The primary clinical manifestation is an expanding erythematous rash (erythema migrans) originating at the bite site. Systemic symptoms may include fever, headache, and fatigue. Without appropriate antibiotic treatment, the infection can progress to involve neurological, articular, and cardiac complications, such as facial palsy, arthritis, severe headaches with neck stiffness, or palpitations. Transmission of the bacterium generally requires the tick to be attached for a period exceeding 24 to 48 hours.

Pro Football Hall of Famer Jerome Bettis issued some strong words for both star running back Le'Veon Bell and the Pittsburgh Steelers as the two sides attempt to work out a long-term deal.
"Neither one of you are as good by yourself as you are together," Bettis said, via TMZ.com.
Bell is set to earn $14.5 million under the franchise tag. He has until the July 16 deadline to finalize a long-term contract.
The 26-year-old Bell, who has been hit with the franchise tag for the second year in a row, missed the majority of the Steelers' offseason last year. He said he is hoping to avoid a repeat of that scenario this summer.
"Le'Veon, you're not going to be as good going somewhere else because they're not going to have the offensive line, they're not going to have the quarterback, the receivers that they have in Pittsburgh," Bettis said. "You have a full complement around you that allows you to be as great as you want to be."
Bell ran for 1,291 yards and a career-high nine touchdowns last season while catching a personal-best 85 passes for 655 yards and two scores. He was third in the NFL in rushing yards and 10th in receptions.
The Steelers finished the 2017 campaign with a 13-3 mark before dropping a 45-42 decision to the Jacksonville Jaguars in the AFC divisional round of the playoffs.
Bettis won a Super Bowl with the Steelers and also played for the then-St. Louis Rams. He retired as the NFL's fifth-best rusher with 13,662 yards and entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

Vancouver police arrested two people at the intersection of Clark Drive and East 1st Avenue Saturday afternoon, after reports of two bank robberies in the area within a half-hour of each other.
Numerous police vehicles responded to the intersection shortly after 2 p.m., when the suspect vehicle - a stolen Porsche Cayenne - crashed into several other vehicles.
Two police vehicles were nearby and were able to block the Cayenne and prevent the suspects inside from escaping, police said.
Police arrested a man and a woman who were inside the suspect vehicle.
Ryland Chernomaz was on Clark Drive at the time of the incident. He said he saw the police vehicles do U-turns and hit the Cayenne, then saw officers get out with their guns drawn.
“He’s on the ground, there’s another girl with him, crying,” Chernomaz said of the moment of the arrest. “I’ve never seen anything like it. Crazy stuff.”
The robberies took place on Commercial Drive and on East Broadway at Commercial.
Four ambulances could be seen at the scene, and police said four people were transported to hospital with minor injuries.
A total of four civilian vehicles were involved in the incident.
Clark Drive was closed for more than an hour as officers from VPD’s Major Crime and Collision Investigation Unit investigated.
rewrite:

This followed reports of two bank robberies occurring within a half-hour timeframe in the vicinity. The incident escalated shortly after 2:00 p.m. when a stolen Porsche Cayenne, identified as the suspect vehicle, collided with several other automobiles. According to police statements, two nearby patrol units responded, maneuvering to block the Cayenne and prevent the occupants from fleeing. A man and a woman inside the vehicle were subsequently taken into custody.

An eyewitness, Ryland Chernomaz, who was present on Clark Drive, reported observing police vehicles execute U-turns before striking the suspect car. He stated that officers then exited with firearms drawn. Chernomaz described the arrest scene, noting one individual on the ground and a female companion crying, remarking on the unprecedented nature of the event. The related robberies occurred on Commercial Drive and at East Broadway and Commercial Drive.

Emergency services, including four ambulances, attended the scene. Four individuals sustained minor injuries and were transported to a hospital. A total of four civilian vehicles were damaged in the collision. Clark Drive was closed for over an hour to facilitate an investigation by the Vancouver Police Department’s Major Crime and Collision Investigation Unit.

Iran has described as “illogical” a move on Sunday by Turkmenistan to halt gas supplies to the country as a result of a row over outstanding debts.
Turkmenistan’s move - that came despite reports of an agreement on Friday over the disputed arrears by the media in Tehran – led to a halt in the activities of several power plants in northern Iran that run on gas.
Officials accordingly ordered a switch to liquid fuel in some of the power plants. Concerns emerged nonetheless that gas supplies in provinces such as Gilan, Mazandaran, and Golestan would not be enough to warm houses with winter already at doorsteps.
At the heart of the dispute between the two countries is a claim by Turkmenistan that Iran owes it $1.8 billion from sales between 2007 and 2008 when freezing winters led to severe shortages across 20 Iranian provinces, forcing the country to raise gas imports from its northeastern neighbor.
At the time, Turkmenistan pounced on the occasion to demand a nine-fold hike which yanked the price up to $360 from $40 for every 1,000 cubic meters of gas.
According to Turkmen officials, the balance has built up to a debt of $1.8 billion which Iran is rejecting and has threatened to take the case to international arbitration.
On Friday, the media in Iran said the two sides had reached an agreement over the dispute.
Officials in Tehran said talks would continue between the two sides over the next few months until a final agreement would be reached.
Iran’s Ministry of Petroleum in a statement on Monday strongly criticized Turkmenistan’s move to cut off supplies of gas to Iran that took place on Sunday morning.
The Ministry described as “illogical” the move which it said was based on a claim that Iran should make a rapid payment of the disputed debt.
It added that Turkmenistan – which it said had also turned the taps on Iran over price disputes during several past winters - had acted against an agreement that had been reached between Tehran and Ashgabat.
The Ministry further called on the nation to reduce consumption to compensate for the loss that a halt in imports from Turkmenistan could create throughout the cold season.
rewrite:
On Sunday, Turkmenistan suspended natural gas exports to Iran, a decision Iranian authorities subsequently characterized as "illogical." This cessation occurred despite reports in Tehran’s media on Friday indicating a provisional agreement had been reached regarding the longstanding debt dispute between the two nations. The immediate consequence of the supply halt was the disruption of operations at several gas-fired power plants in northern Iran. In response, officials mandated a switch to liquid fuel at some facilities. Nevertheless, concerns arose regarding the adequacy of gas supplies for residential heating in northern provinces such as Gilan, Mazandaran, and Golestan, particularly with the imminent onset of winter.

The core of the bilateral disagreement stems from Turkmenistan’s assertion that Iran accrued a debt of $1.8 billion for gas imports between 2007 and 2008. During that period, severe winter conditions precipitated critical gas shortages across approximately twenty Iranian provinces, compelling Iran to significantly increase imports from its northeastern neighbor. Exploiting this heightened demand, Turkmenistan instituted a substantial price increase, raising the cost from $40 to $360 per 1,000 cubic meters. Turkmen officials maintain that the outstanding balance from this period has accumulated to the cited $1.8 billion. Iran disputes both the validity and the magnitude of this claimed debt and has threatened to seek international arbitration for resolution.

Contrary to the Sunday suspension, Iranian media had reported a bilateral agreement on the dispute the preceding Friday. Iranian officials indicated that negotiations would continue over subsequent months to finalize a settlement. In a formal statement issued Monday, Iran’s Ministry of Petroleum strongly condemned Turkmenistan’s decision to sever gas supplies that previous morning. The Ministry deemed the action "illogical," arguing it was predicated on an unjustified demand for immediate payment of the contested sum. Furthermore, the statement accused Turkmenistan of violating a recently established agreement between Tehran and Ashgabat, noting a history of similar supply interruptions during past winters over pricing conflicts. To mitigate the potential shortfall throughout the cold season, the Ministry issued a public appeal for reduced domestic gas consumption to compensate for the halted imports from Turkmenistan.

Motorists and technicians alike are always looking for ways to extend engine life and restore engine performance to original levels. Penray Inc. says it has introduced two new chemical service kits that do exactly that.
Penray’s new two-step Oil and Fuel Treatment Kit No. 7702 offers a simple-to-use chemical service kit that removes debris and deposits from fuel systems, while fortifying engine oil with a specially-formulated compound that strengthens and extends the life of engine oil. The combination of these two products enhances the effectiveness of any oil change service.
Penray also is introducing an upgraded three-step Premium Oil System Cleaner kit, No. 7603. This new kit includes the same oil and fuel supplements as the two-step kit, and adds Penray’s Crankcase and Differential Cleaner. This powerful cleaning agent is particularly useful on higher-mileage engines, those which have seen severe service or those that have not had regular oil and filter changes. This cleaner is designed to be added to engine oil five minutes before draining, and works to dissolve gum, sludge and varnish throughout the crankcase, including critical areas like pistons, rings, cylinder walls and the highly-sensitive cam/lifter interface.
“These two new chemical service kits, created and manufactured in the United States, represent an important opportunity to upgrade a routine oil change into a premium engine service,” said Mark Kardon, director of marketing for Penray. “The precision of fuel injectors used in virtually all late-model cars requires that they be kept meticulously clean and free of debris and deposits that can interfere with proper fuel delivery and injector spray patterns. These two new service kits provide the opportunity to upgrade to a powerful premium service that enhances both performance and longevity.”

Business News of Friday, 6 October 2017
Source: thebftonline.com
2017-10-06
File photo: Government to pull down buildings that do not meet building requirements
Indiscriminately constructed buildings which do not conform to the required building regulations are likely to be pulled down when government completes amending the building code.
“The building everywhere and anyhow mentality cannot continue with the passage and enforcement of the law we pray this august house will make,” Works and Housing Minister, Samuel Atta Akyea, told parliament on World Habitat Day celebrated on October 2.
The ministry, he said, is in the process of amending the Building Regulations LI 1630 of 1996 to reflect the revised Building Code.
The Draft Ghana Building Code, which was put together by the Building and Road Research Institute (BRRI) in 1988, has been reviewed by the Ministry of Works and Housing and its stakeholders and is ready for adoption.
The minister also disclosed that in view of the increasing demand for the development of high rise buildings and its implications for shared ownership of common areas, and also to maximise limited land space, the ministry is seeking cabinet approval before a final bill on condominium properties is drafted by the Attorney General’s Department.
Government is determined to address the housing deficit, through partnerships with the private sector in the provision of affordable housing units of different typologies to meet the demands of Ghanaians, he said.
The Ministry of Works and Housing is implementing the Affordable Housing Programme aimed at providing adequate, decent affordable housing, particularly to low- and middle-income groups.
Recognising low income levels as a challenge on the demand side of housing in Ghana, the ministry’s focus is how to make housing affordable. To achieve this goal, “We are adopting cost-saving technologies and new techniques of construction, as well as innovative mortgage financing,” he added.
One of the major bottlenecks facing housing delivery in Ghana is financing. Government is therefore adopting a two-pronged approach to mobilise funds both domestically and internationally to support the Housing sector.
rewrite:
On October 6, 2017, the Minister for Works and Housing, Samuel Atta Akyea, addressed the Parliament of Ghana in observance of World Habitat Day. In his statement, the minister outlined several forthcoming legislative and policy initiatives aimed at reforming the nation’s built environment and addressing its housing deficit.

A primary focus of the address was the imminent revision of national building regulations. The minister indicated that the Ministry of Works and Housing is in the process of amending the existing Building Regulations, LI 1630 of 1996, to align with a revised national Building Code. This revised code, originally drafted by the Building and Road Research Institute (BRRI) in 1988, has undergone a comprehensive review by the ministry and relevant stakeholders and is now prepared for formal adoption. Minister Atta Akyea emphasized that upon the passage and enforcement of the updated law, structures erected indiscriminately and in violation of the new regulatory standards would be subject to demolition.

Concurrently, the ministry is pursuing the development of a legal framework for condominium properties. This initiative is driven by the growing demand for high-rise developments, which present implications for the shared ownership of common areas and offer a means to maximize limited urban land space. The minister disclosed that the proposal is awaiting cabinet approval prior to the drafting of a final bill by the Attorney General’s Department.

To tackle the broader national housing shortage, the government is committed to fostering public-private partnerships for the provision of diverse, affordable housing typologies. The Ministry of Works and Housing is implementing an Affordable Housing Programme specifically targeted at low- and middle-income groups. Acknowledging that low income levels constrain effective demand, the ministry’s strategy incorporates the adoption of cost-saving construction technologies and innovative mortgage financing models.

Financing remains a critical bottleneck for housing delivery. To this end, the government is adopting a dual approach to mobilize capital, seeking both domestic and international funding streams to support the sector’s growth.
